For the past six months, I've been on a quiet personal mission — reading books, completing hands-on training, and watching more hours of technical content than I'd like to admit, all in an attempt to bring meaningful AI capabilities to my team as a cybersecurity manager with no AI engineering background. Of all the resources I leaned on, the AI Engineer YouTube channel was a key source of knowledge and inspiration. So when I heard that AI Engineer was coming to Singapore, clearing my weekend wasn't even a question.

I came with two questions: how can I up my "Personal AI agents" game to be more productive, and what does it look like for a team to genuinely become AI-native? Three days in. Here's what stayed with me:

🧱 1. The Fundamental Building Blocks for an AI-native Team:
The common thread across Belli's leadership track talk (by Jeff Pan and Alex Khor) and Conor Brennan-Burke's session was this: before you reach for agents, you need the right foundation in place — the knowledge, know-how, skills, and context that make up your Company Brain. Agents are only as useful as the context they can draw from. Getting that layer right first is the actual work. Jeff's analogy landed with me: 19th-century Paris was killing people because clean and dirty water mixed. Haussmann fixed the infrastructure first, before anything else was built on top of it. That system still runs beneath Paris today. The same principle applies when building an AI-native team.

🏭 2. Building Our Own Software Factories:
Nick Miller from Cursor leadership talk and workshop reframed something for me. The concept of a software factory — cloud agents that run independently, tackle larger tasks over longer timescales, and return with reviewable artefacts. What follows is a significant shift in roles: individual contributors spend less time building from scratch, and managers spend more time reviewing, directing, and making judgment calls. What if we can apply the same concept to cybersecurity workflows?

🤝 3. Conversations You Can't Get From YouTube or Books:
Between sessions, over coffee, and at the side events before AI Engineering conference, I got to speak with people who were already deep in it — building their own personal agents, running AI-native teams, or actively in the middle of that transition. Hearing how they structure their workflows, what broke, what stuck, and what they'd do differently was the kind of learning no YouTube video can replicate. I left with more ideas than I could fit in a notebook, and a much clearer picture of what's actually possible when you stop theorising and start doing.

To 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Rachael De Foe, and the entire 65Labs team — thank you for making this happen in Singapore. The access to speakers, the conversations between sessions, and the quality of the community in that room made this genuinely worth the three days. Anticipating AI Engineer Singapore 2027!
#AIEngineerSingapore #65Labs #AIEngineer #PersonalAgents

Still thinking about what came out of AI Engineer Singapore [https://lnkd.in/gZZwmY58] over the weekend

Five things that actually shifted how I think:
1. Stop using LLMs as a single router.
JJ Geewax (Google DeepMind) said it plainly: break your system into smaller deterministic pieces. Transform → Route → Transform → Generate → Safety Check. Don't shove everything into one system prompt and hope. This directly changed how I'm structuring my tools.

2. The blocker is no longer the technology. It's leadership.
Andy Brown (OpenAI) gave his whole team Codex access and said just try it. Geoffrey Huntley put it sharper: the marginal cost of building a new tool is now approaching zero. The only thing stopping most organizations is leaders who haven't built anything themselves.
Best ideas + real domain experience + willingness to actually build = the new moat.

3. Sandbox your agents. Prompting harder doesn't fix reliability.
Tejas Kumar (IBM) demonstrated live: same agent, same model, same prompt — completely different outcomes just by building a proper harness around it. Guardrails, verification layers, intervention points. Build better guardrails. Don't prompt harder.

4. Measure problems solved. Not tokens consumed.
Zixuan Li (Z.AI) flipped the framing: token consumption leaderboards are Goodhart's Law in action. The real question is how much work got done, how much efficiency actually gained. His team doesn't DM — only group channels, so AI always has full context. The org isn't adopting AI. The org is becoming context for AI.

5. Wisdom filters beat prompt engineering.
A founder in the Leadership Track shared how their agent once offered a free pilot for a massive assembly line — over WhatsApp. Their fix: a fine-tuned wisdom model that verifies every agent output before it reaches a customer. Not more prompting. A separate verification layer trained on what "good" actually looks like. Underused. Immediately replicable.

I lead commerce at EMTEK group and building on the #1 social commerce platform in the world — creators, brand partnerships, monetization. I've been building AI tools to automate how we operate. Three more shipping in the next 90 days using Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Cursor.
The infrastructure is there. The question is whether leaders actually pick it up.
Thanks to Sherry Jiang and Tomas Laboutka and the whole 65Labs team. First AI Engineer in Asia. Won't be the last.

I spent the weekend volunteering at AI Engineer Singapore 2026! 💻🚀🇸🇬

My background shaped how I experienced the conference: building design/workflow tools as a developer, and working in customer-facing technical roles across selling, scoping, demos, and production rollout.
So I listened from the perspective of someone bridging technology and customer reality:

What actually holds up in production? How do we explain that clearly to customers?

Here are 3 things that stood out to me the most.

🤖 1. Agentic AI is now the default
Greptile shared that 27.6% of April 2026 PRs across 65K organizations showed strong evidence of being fully AI-authored, up from under 1% a year earlier. Stripe’s “Minions” agents merge 3K+ PRs/week at a 65% one-shot merge rate. Vercel highlighted that the SDLC bottleneck has moved from build to review, validation, and deployment.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Customers aren’t asking whether to adopt agents anymore. Many already have. The question is now: “How do we manage what we’ve unleashed?”

🔒 2. Agents will get compromised — design for it
Daytona, NanoClaw, and Tusk all pointed to the same principle: instructions are not security. The real defense is architecture — keep secrets outside the agent, restrict access, separate tool calls from execution, and log every request.
The Swiss Cheese Model came up repeatedly: no single layer is perfect, so stack defenses so the holes don’t line up.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: “Is AI safe?” often stalls enterprise deals. It’s not just a product question — it’s an architecture question.

📏 3. You can’t ship agents without evals
Arize AI framed it clearly: “Traces are logs. Evals are tests.” The talk covered Code, LLM, Human, and Agent Evals, plus the “March of Nines” — a reminder that getting AI systems from “mostly works” to enterprise-grade reliability is a long operational grind, especially when customers expect near-perfect consistency, safety, and predictability in production.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Many customers have agents, but no clear way to measure them. Helping design evals during the POC helps build the internal case for production.

My takeaway:
As AI agents become capable of handling more and more individual tasks, the value of humans shifts toward ownership, judgment, and orchestration.
The people customers will trust most won’t be the ones who simply know the latest models or tools. They’ll be the ones who understand a customer’s workflow end-to-end — knowing where AI should operate autonomously, where humans must stay in the loop, and how to combine the right systems, safeguards, and tools into something customers can actually trust in production.

If this resonates, I’d love to compare notes.

Huge shoutout to 65labs Labs for bringing this together!

I am not a developer, but I think that is exactly why it was useful to be there.

Every company, function, and leadership team needs to start thinking AI-first. Not by forcing AI into every workflow, but by understanding:

💡 Where it can improve productivity
💡 Where it can raise the quality of output
💡 Where it can simplify tasks that today take too much time
💡 Where it can help teams move faster, with more context and less friction

Across the conference, it was great to see how broad the AI landscape has become:
🤖 Robotics
🛠 Debugging and coding tools
🧠 Agentic workflows
🏗 Developer infrastructure

posts.text: Built a lot in one day at AI Engineer Singapore (Day 1) — equal parts “systems thinking” and “ship it.” What I learned / took away: • Vercel v0 workshop: the stack for shipping AI apps is maturing fast — AI gateway for routing/observability + SDKs/components for streaming UX, plus a push toward “agent-ready” experiences (AEO = Answer Engine Optimization). • Cursor workshop: the idea of a software factory really clicked — moving from “AI pair programmer” to asynchronous cloud agents that create PRs, run checks, and get reviewed with guardrails (tests/hooks/rules/skills). The engineer’s job shifts toward specs, reviews, and building the factory. • OpenAI FDE approach: strong reminder that the hardest part isn’t the model — it’s discovery + iteration + evaluation early. When the space is still nascent, you need people who can go from first principles to production and feed learnings back into product/research. • Cloudflare workshop: loved the framing of why traditional MCP workflows get expensive/slow (stateless models + repeated context + many round trips) and how Code Mode can compress that into a single TypeScript “plan” with logic. Also: Workers + Durable Objects make a lot of sense for stateful agent experiences. • Stick 'Em AI-powered robotics workshop: the most fun part — hands-on building + coding under time pressure. Vibe-coded a “Mood Monster” robot with a new friend Yezi Zhu in ~1 hour. Built fast, iterated faster, and somehow it worked (photos in the post). If you’re building agents/products this year, the theme feels clear: better primitives, better workflows, better evaluation — and more time spent on the “factory,” not just the code.

With special thanks to Boonsri Srinivasan we just finished producing a behind-the-scenes video about Tesseract Mindflow at ai.engineer Singapore.

Watching back the footage from yesterday, I realised this project has evolved into something far beyond where it originally started.

Tesseract Mindflow and our broader Synthaesthetic Art work began as a creative exploration around a simple question:

Could AI, robotics, and brain-computer interfaces give people new forms of creative expression instead of taking creativity away?

At ai.engineer this week, we brought that idea onto the stage live.

Backstage at the Capitol Kempinski Theatre, surrounded by robot arms, EEG headsets, paintbrushes, OSC messages, laptops, cables, and a fairly terrifying live-demo countdown timer, our team prepared for a demonstration where Kai Ming N. would paint using our brain-controlled robotic system.

Kai Ming lives with a degenerative condition that has progressively reduced the dexterity in her hands and fingers. Painting, something closely connected to her family, identity, and childhood, had gradually become inaccessible.

What happened on stage was a collaboration between human intent, AI systems, robotics, and shared autonomy.

Brain signals were processed in real time and connected into a robotic painting system, allowing Kai Ming to once again participate directly in the act of painting and creative expression.

Not as a passive observer of technology, but as a connected artist.

One of the most important things Kai Ming said during filming was that conversations around AI are often dominated by fear, replacement, and uncertainty, while much less attention is given to the ways these technologies can empower people and restore participation.

That concept is what has motivated the whole team throughout this project.

Standing backstage before the session, this genuinely did not feel like “just another tech demo.”

It felt like a small glimpse into a future where AI systems help more people participate in creativity, work, communication, and self-expression.

Huge thank you to everyone involved:

Kai Ming N. for trusting us with something deeply personal and for sharing her story publicly.

Ivy Chen for helping shape the artistic direction and broader vision of Synthaesthetic Art from the beginning.

Jackie Tan for helping make an incredibly complex live system somehow survive conference conditions.

Dr Richard Savery who has been working alongside me on these ideas for years, from the earliest concepts around human-machine creative collaboration through to what just happened on stage.

The future of AI does not need to be humans versus machines.

There is another path emerging where humans and machines create together.

“Tesseract Mindflow: amplifying human creativity through shared autonomy.”

#AIEngineer #Singapore, Day 1. Back at Singapore Management University — not for school, but to learn. Here to learn what builders are actually shipping, not to be sold to. The workshop format is allergic to pitch decks. That's why the signal-to-noise on the floor beats anything on the keynote stage. What stood out: ✅ Mastra — Sam Bhagwat building a durable-execution layer on top of agentic orchestration. The right altitude. Most of the agent stack still treats durability as an afterthought; he's treating it as the substrate. ✅ Stripe + Amazon Web Services (AWS) — pushing #MPP for agent-fiat payments. The card-backed wave, dressed up for the agent economy. ✅ Arize AI — an eval harness for the eval loop. The discipline most enterprise AI deployments skip and regret. ✅ #CLI over #MCP — The crowd is starting to move away from #MCP, to save on tokens. What's missing, though, is the story: ❌ No #x402, no #stablecoin acceptance. Stripe pushed #MPP on fiat rails; Coinbase wasn't in the room. The agent-economy payment conversation today is a card-backed conversation. That's half the board. ❌ No alternate payment methods. Cards, cards, cards. Nothing on #A2A, direct debit, regional rails, or #stablecoin settlement — the methods that actually carry most cross-border B2B today. ❌ No Anthropic. Heavy OpenAI presence, no Anthropic counter-voice. For a builder floor that prides itself on neutrality, one frontier lab louder than the other is a balance problem. ❌ The autonomy line is undrawn. Autonomous orchestration (CrewAI) vs. structured workflows (n8n) — the room treats observability as the answer to both. Observability, durability, evaluation, and autonomy are four different problems. Nobody's named where one ends and the next begins. A workshop floor is a leading indicator: what's on it tells you what's being built; what's off it tells you what's being missed. If you're building agent-economy payments outside the card-backed stack — stablecoin acceptance, #x402, #AP2, #A2A rails — DM me. If you're in the room for Days 2 and 3 and reading the gaps differently, push back in the comments. #AIEngineerSingapore #AgenticAI #PaymentsInfrastructure #x402 #AgentEconomy Sounds like real Fun Joel. We are working on x402 for agentic payment at loomal.ai Let's connect to speak soon!

이번 봄, Nitro Seoul을 통해 한국의 AI 빌더들과 몇 달간 함께하며 다시 한 번 또렷해진 한 가지가 있습니다. 우리에게 글로벌은 다음 단계가 아닙니다. Day 1부터 default입니다.

그래서 모두에게 가장 중요한 것도 바뀌고 있다고 봅니다. 단순 자본이 아니라, 같은 속도로 일하는 빌더들과 같은 도시에서 함께 마주 앉을 자리, 이것이 점점 더 핵심 자원이 되어가는 것 같습니다.

Hashed는 기술이 산업의 경계를 다시 그리는 순간마다 그 변화를 만드는 창업자들과 가장 이른 시점에 함께 일해 왔습니다. 초연결 시대로의 전환을 보다 일찍 목격하며 샌프란시스코, 싱가포르, 벵갈루루, 방콕, 아부다비에 차례로 자리를 잡았고, 저는 그 흐름의 일부로 싱가포르를 베이스로 여러 도시를 오가며 지내고 있습니다.

지난 몇 년 사이 싱가포르는 글로벌 AI 회사들의 아시아 거점이 가장 밀집한 도시가 되었고, 아시아에서 AI 인재 풀이 가장 빠르게 성장한 곳이 되었습니다. 한국 빌더들이 마주 앉기에 자연스러운 도시 중 하나가 됐다는 뜻이기도 합니다.

Goobong Jeong님의 Ralphthon이 흥미로운 건 해커톤이라서가 아닙니다. 평가축이 다릅니다. 최고의 코더가 아니라 최고의 delegator가 이기는 포맷이고, 랩탑을 직접 만진 횟수가 적을수록 점수가 올라갑니다. 코드는 부산물이고, 사람들이 서로를 만나는 것이 본질이라고 선언하는, 지금은 조금 생소하다고 느껴져도 곧 스탠다드가 될 포맷입니다. 서울과 샌프란시스코에서 검증된 이 이벤트가 이번 주말 처음으로 싱가포르에 도착합니다.

저희가 싱가포르에 있는 이유는 정확히 이런 순간들을 위한 것이라고 생각합니다. 이번 행사를 위해 짧은 시간 안에 싱가포르의 좋은 파트너들이 모이는 과정 자체가 이 씬이 얼마나 가까워졌는지 보여주는 증거였다고 생각합니다.

في مؤتمر AI Engineer Singapore، شارك الدكتور Vivian Balakrishnan، وزير الخارجية السنغافوري، تجربته الشخصية في بناء “دماغ ثانٍ” (Second Brain) بالذكاء الاصطناعي مخصص للدبلوماسية. 

استخدم وزير الخارجية جهاز Raspberry Pi بسيط، ودمج Claude AI مع تكامل WhatsApp، وذاكرة محلية دائمة (knowledge graph)، وأدوات مثل NanoClaw و Obsidian. هذا النظام يساعده في:

- إدارة الحمل المعرفي الهائل أثناء السفر والاجتماعات الدولية
- تلخيص التقارير والمقالات
- صياغة الخطب
- البحث السريع وتحليل البيانات

الرسالة الأقوى التي أطلقها:  
“لا يمكنك حكم تقنية لم تتعامل معها إلا من خلال إحاطات نظرية”  
“You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.”

هذا المثال يعكس فلسفة “تعلم بالممارسة” (learn by doing)، ويؤكد أن القيمة الحقيقية للذكاء الاصطناعي تأتي من التخصيص والتكامل مع سير العمل اليومي، وليس فقط من النماذج الحدودية الكبيرة.

سنغافورة تثبت مرة أخرى أن القيادة الحقيقية في عصر الذكاء الاصطناعي تبدأ بالتجربة العملية والشجاعة في البناء.

شاهدوا الفيديو المرفق لتفاصيل أكثر إلهامًا! 🎥

posts.text:
The conversations after AI Engineer Singapore were just as important as the conference itself.

This week wasn’t only about AI presentations, product demos, or keynote sessions. The real value came from the side events, founder dinners, community mixers, and late-night conversations where builders openly discussed what is actually happening in AI today.

At Insight Genesis - IGAi Genesis, these conversations reinforced something we strongly believe:

The future of AI will not just be about generating content.
It will be about generating meaningful human insights from data.
We are moving into an era where AI can understand behavior, wellness, intent, patterns, decision-making, and human interaction at a much deeper level. The next evolution of AI is not only intelligence — it is contextual intelligence powered by data correlation, behavioral analytics, and decentralized ownership.
Throughout the week, we had discussions with AI engineers, founders, investors, healthcare innovators, Web3 builders, and enterprise operators exploring how AI can transform industries through better understanding of people and data.

Some of the biggest conversations centered around:
• AI agents and autonomous systems
• Behavioral intelligence and predictive analytics
• AI infrastructure and data ownership
• Personalized AI-driven decision making
• Privacy-first AI ecosystems
• AI + Web3 convergence
• Real-world deployment over hype

What became very clear is that organizations are no longer looking for isolated AI tools. They are looking for AI systems that can connect fragmented data, generate actionable intelligence, and create real utility.

That is exactly the direction we are building toward at Insight Genesis - IGAi 
Our mission is to transform disconnected data into meaningful decentralized personal insights — enabling individuals and organizations to unlock deeper understanding through AI-powered analytics, behavioral intelligence, and privacy-first infrastructure. The platform combines AI analytics, voice analysis, video analysis, and decentralized data ownership to create actionable human-centric insights. (Insight Genesis Docs)

Singapore is rapidly becoming one of the most important hubs for AI innovation in Asia because it brings together global talent, capital, enterprise adoption, and startup ecosystems in one place.
The side events reminded us that innovation rarely happens in isolation.
It happens through conversations.

Huge respect to everyone contributing to this growing ecosystem — organizers, founders, engineers, researchers, creators, and investors.
The momentum around AI is accelerating rapidly, and we are only at the beginning of what’s coming next. 🚀

Product Gym is live at daily.deepikamurthy.com. I built it as part of a AIE Singapore hackathon, and I've always wanted to build something on Lenny's data. Thanks to Lenny Rachitsky for making his content available to build with!

Try to get on the leaderboard, new hat to wear everyday!

Two products got me here.

The first was Mindgym,https://lnkd.in/gxyqsprw by Khushboo Maheshwari an Indian product my son tried and loved. Kids work through a daily problem-solving exercise and it builds their thinking skills. The format stuck with me, a case study followed by diagnostic questions. Lenny's content is long-form and I kept asking, how do you know if you've actually understood it? Can you apply it? What helps recall?

The second was the daily-habit loop where you solve something and share the result. Wordle does this well. I mixed that with the Mindgym format and Product Gym is what came out.

Putting it in the wild to see how it performs. A few things to call out.

It's built by a solo PM trying to cover every use case end-to-end. There will be bugs, please report them.

If the cases don't feel compelling to solve, tell me that too.

On question quality, I used Claude with a prompt I've tested and reviewed, but it can still produce cases or learnings that aren't meaningful. Flag those.

I want to thank the folks who inspired this and Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh and Brian C. for enabling this with the hackathon.

posts.text: i never set out to be a community person. i'm a builder at heart. for over 10 years i've been obsessed with creating beautiful yet useful product experiences - the kind that make people feel empowered. that's still what i do every day. but while building my own company, i started learning to code with ai. and i started sharing what i was learning online. then something unexpected happened. people didn't just want the content - they wanted to be in the room, building together. that's what started code with ai. then the meetups. then hackathons. and now a full-blown conference - ai engineer, the largest builder-focused ai event - coming to singapore for the first time. and tbh i'm still stunned by the impact: - people finding jobs through connections made at our events - teams that formed at hackathons turning into actual companies - builders in vietnam and malaysia and beyond starting their own hackathons after seeing ours and in hindsight, the gap was always obvious. there are incredibly talented builders in singapore and southeast asia. they just need to be seen. i'm so grateful for my co-organizers who are building ai engineer singapore alongside me. all of us do this on an almost volunteer basis - nights, weekends, on top of our full-time jobs, sometimes putting in our own money to make sure things actually happen. and we do this because we deeply believe that the work happening here deserves a world-class stage. and we're building it. cue the "we-are-so-back" It's been amazing watching you and the 65labs team smashing it over the past year: meetups, coding, hackathons, courses (some DJ'ing too) and now the best conference of 2026! Literally building the AI builder community in Singapore 😎 👏 👏 👏 Nice one sherry ❤️❤️ Sherry Jiang This is amazing! Love how you’re turning learning into a community and giving builders in SEA the stage they deserve. Excited to see the impact continue! 🙌 Very nice and natural evolution. Keep going and keep building! Thank you Sherry Jiang & 🥃 Agrim Singh for creating this really special and amazing community that elevates everyday people who want to learn and build with AI. It's really something special you've both have grown! The community you're building is amazing, Sherry Jiang!! Inspiring!

posts.text: Update: all 20 student tickets are covered!! When the sponsor pulled out, we decided to take on the first 10 tickets ourselves. Then we asked if anyone wanted to help get the other 10 students in. You did. Some people covered a full ticket. Some chipped in part of one. Some just DM’d, "How much is left?" So yes, 20 students are now coming to AI Engineer Singapore. And honestly, we’re still a bit emotional about it. ❤️🩹 I asked a few of the folks who contributed to share why they chose to back Singapore’s next wave of AI builders. You don’t have to read every slide, but… If you’re a student, I hope you read enough to know this: People already in the room believe you belong there too. And if you’re not a student, maybe this is a reminder that backing the ecosystem doesn’t always have to be a big institutional gesture. Sometimes it’s opening a door because someone once opened one for you. Thank you to everyone who helped turn a really disappointing moment into something so, so generous. Today I tried something that genuinely made me pause for a second.

Inspired by Gabriel Chua Codex OpenAI session at AI Engineer Singapore, I gave a simple instruction to Codex from my iPhone while travelling back from the event:

“Pick the best photos from today’s event from my Photos folder, use royalty-free music, create a short 20-second video recap and upload it somewhere I can review.”

That’s it.

No editing timeline.
No manually selecting clips.
No opening Final Cut.
No moving files around.

The interesting part wasn’t even the video generation.

It was the reasoning.

Codex figured out I was prompting from my phone and did not have direct access to the files sitting locally on my Mac Mini. So it suggested using iCloud upload flow automatically so I could review the generated video from my phone.

That small moment honestly blew my mind.

The first version was not perfect. It missed some images and audio timing was off. But after a few iterations and steering the agent a bit more, it got surprisingly good.

And the crazy part?

While I was moving around the city after the event, the machine at home was literally working for me.

This was probably the biggest mindset shift for me from the conference:

AI is no longer just “answering questions.”

It is starting to:
- operate tools
- reason across environments
- understand context
- recover from constraints
- orchestrate workflows
- execute tasks asynchronously

At the table today, many engineers discussed whether AI replaces developers.

My takeaway was slightly different.

The biggest risk is probably not “AI replacing developers.”

It’s developers, PMs, designers, analysts, and really every knowledge worker not adapting to this new way of working.

The people who learn how to orchestrate these systems early are going to operate very differently in the next few years.

Still processing how fast things are moving.

Shout out to 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang Brian C. from 65labs for an awesome event. 

Curious mind. Builder mode! 🇸🇬

posts.text:
Day 1 at AI Engineer Singapore was honestly one of the most eye-opening AI events I’ve attended so far.

https://lnkd.in/gHn4GtWh → Made a small recap video of Day 1.

Biggest realization: AI is rapidly shifting from “just prompting models” to building full systems around agents, evals, feedback loops, infrastructure, and developer workflows.

Started the day with Exa talking about real-time research agents and web-scale search.

The easiest way to describe Exa:
AI agents need their own version of Google.

Exa acts as a search and retrieval layer for AI systems, helping agents retrieve fresh and reliable web information in real time. Super useful for research agents, RAG systems, and AI-powered products.

They also showcased Websets, where instead of manually researching and building spreadsheets yourself, you can describe what you want in plain English and AI agents will search the web and structure the results automatically into spreadsheets.

Later, I attended a session by Cursor where Nick Miller talked about the future of AI-driven software development and “software factories.”

One analogy that really stood out:
Software factories are not mass production factories.
They are more like Michelin-star kitchens.

Highly automated, but still requiring engineering craftsmanship, oversight, testing, and validation.

Some interesting ideas from the talk:

* Cloud-based coding agents running builds/tests in isolated VMs
* Always-on PR review agents like BugBot
* READMEs, workflows, and reusable “skills” becoming increasingly important for AI agents
* Reliable testing environments still being critical even in AI-assisted workflows

During networking, I also had a great conversation with Max Buckley about how students can now quickly “vibe code” products with AI, but real engineering environments still require strong reliability, maintainability, testing, and validation standards.

The final talk I attended was by Fuad A. from Arize AI:

“Ship Real Agents: Evals, Traces, and the Production Feedback Loop.”

One big takeaway from the talk was that evals are becoming one of the most important parts of building AI products. It is no longer just about prompting models, but about building strong feedback loops, tracing outputs, improving datasets, and continuously iterating on systems.

Also had an amazing time meeting people throughout the event, including Cheng Ye, Lavanya Garg, Lucius Chee, Jesmine Goh and Teck Leong Fong.

Really excited for Day 2 tomorrow 🚀

posts.text:
The AI bottleneck is not generation. It is verification. 

💡Some fresh learnings from an amazing AI Engineer 🇸🇬 weekend

It’s not model selection. Not prompt quality. Not the tooling stack. Once you can generate code faster than your team can read it, the scarce resource is the judgment layer - the ability to know whether what you built is actually right.

A few other things that stayed with me from the weekend:

1. Engineers are becoming fleet managers. The unit of work is shifting from a ticket to a spec. If your team cannot write clear, bounded specs, agents cannot help you.

2. The org design question to ask - if contributing context to AI systems is the new unit of value, what happens to the parts of your organisation that cannot do that?

3. The gap is no longer model capability. It is deployment. Intelligence is now abundant. The constraint is whether your organisation can actually use it.

4. If the leaders in your organisation are not using the tools themselves, the transformation stalls. Every speaker who had seen it work said the same thing: top-down personal adoption, not just top-down mandate. 

“You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.”

Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan exemplified this in his opening speech  (https://lnkd.in/gjB9-z3P)

5. No model is permanent. If your system is built around one, you are not building infrastructure - you are taking a position. Keep the framework model-agnostic. Build those harnesses.

What we shipped together at the 65labs x AI Engineer Hackathon in Singapore this weekend.

I saw the hackathon Friday morning, signed up immediately, and booked a flight to Singapore 4 hours before departure. Landed Saturday 6am and started hacking at National University of Singapore campus by 8:30 - no sleep, full conviction.

We initially scoped systems and infra ideas for running AI models, but with under 3 hours left we made the call to pivot and shipped MyKo instead. Recorded the demo in the final 3 minutes ( mic was off, no wayy).

We didn't make it to the finals, but not making it didn't slow us down. If anything, it sharpened what we took away: how to scope under pressure, when to pivot, and how to ship when the clock is the only thing left on your side.

Amelia Low and Amruta Gurav i learned a lot from both of you in a very short time. Grateful we ended up on the same team. And thanks to the 65labs and AI Engineer crew for making these all happen.

Just fly out. Do the thing. ⚡🇸🇬

#AIEngineer #Hackathon #Singapore #OpenAI #GPT5

Every morning at 9am, Claude briefs me on Enterprise AI across the region. Every morning, the same story: Singapore is accelerating. Today, I saw exactly how much.

I watched Singapore's Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan present on stage at AI Engineer Singapore about his personal AI agent, what he calls a 'second brain for diplomats.'

In a single month, Dr. Vivian travels to at least 14 different countries. Every meeting demands a deep, layered context of the people and country he visits.

That is an extraordinary cognitive load for a person, so he built a system that is a living knowledge graph of everything he reads and receives - using open-source tools, running on a Raspberry Pi 5 in his home.

The ripple effect of a public figure at this level taking that step is significant. It sets a precedent and signals to every organisation in the region that hands-on engagement with AI isn't just for technical teams, it's a leadership responsibility.

I'd like to highlight some gems from the session;

 "Real value is created when ordinary people- teachers, managers, engineers, doctors, lawyers, and even ministers are provided with AI tools that transform how they get their job done."

"You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on."

As we move from AI's aspirational productivity gains into concrete economic gains, these are the parameters that would set industries and nations apart - ordinary people doing the extraordinary with AI.

Watching Dr.Vivian stand on stage and show us what genuine AI fluency at the highest level looks like was refreshing and reflects the nation's grand ambitions in AI adoption and policy.

Follow for more #AgenticAI #AILeadership #EnterpriseAI #FutureOfWork #AIStrategy developments in Southeast Asia.

Where in the world can you find a senior government leader with a personal AI stack published on GitHub? How many would be willing to talk about it in a room full of builders? Which is why we are so incredibly honoured to welcome Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to the lineup of speakers for AI Engineer Singapore. A few weeks ago, Minister Balakrishnan casually dropped a technical writeup of his personal AI system online. Raspberry Pi. Claude. Local embeddings. Knowledge graphs. A full architecture breakdown. In a role that demands navigating enormous volumes of information and constant context-switching, his reflections will set the tone for the conference in exactly the way we hoped: That meaningful conversations about AI should not stay abstract. Three days at #AI #Engineer #Singapore. Walked in wondering, “Is the agent thing real for enterprises yet?” and walked out with a different question: how fast can incumbents actually absorb it⁉️

THE SCENE:
➡️ #Stripe: 91% of engineers use AI daily; 100% somewhere in the authoring lifecycle. Their internal one-shot coding agent, “Minion,” opens around 3,000 PRs per week, and 65% merge first-try with no human in the loop. Slack-to-PR.

➡️ #Cursor described what they call the “Dark Software Factory” — engineers shifting from ICs to managers of cloud agents. Their pitch: write the rules, build the harness, let agents run async. Composer 2 ships PRs at $0.35 per task.

➡️ #GovTech Singapore is moving from “AI-enabled” to “AI-native” — all 150,000 public officers, plus a Sovereign Agentic Harness: MCP gateway, agent identity, memory, skills, and observability. Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, demoed a personal agent he built himself on a Raspberry Pi to manage his own workload. His line: “You cannot govern a technology you’ve only been briefed on.” The same logic applies to every CTO.

➡️ #Cognition (#Devin) just announced Singapore as their APAC HQ. Swyx put a sharp point on the enterprise opportunity: local banks running 2M+ lines of undocumented COBOL, $100M AI budgets sitting unspent, and AI-engineering demand around 4x supply in Singapore.

➡️ #LlamaIndex shared what production really looks like at a billion+ documents: white-space output loops, provider outages “almost daily,” and models hallucinating “Delaware incorporation documents” on empty input. The enterprise playbook is multi-model failover, deterministic non-LLM fallbacks such as LiteParse, and serious evals such as ParseBench.

➡️ #Sonar’s ACDC: Guide / Verify / Solve. #Arize for agent observability and evals in CI/CD. #Tusk’s Fence for OS-level deterministic policy enforcement. #Daytona for per-agent runtime isolation. IBM’s #OpenRAG for enterprise document agents. The “agent platform” stack for regulated enterprises is materializing fast.

TAKEAWAYS for Client Convos:

1. The bottleneck in enterprise AI is no longer the model. It’s context, evals, and a harness you trust in regulated environments.

2. Lean teams with strong harnesses outperform large teams trying to retrofit AI onto legacy process.

3. For regulated verticals such as banking, public sector, the partnership pattern is clear: bring #domain_knowledge and #golden_datasets and #rent the platform. Don’t roll your own.

What an overload of amazing content. Lucky I had my second #agent #brain in the works to process and extract these takeaways...
Congrats 65labs Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh and all the builders that showed up!

posts.text:
Today, I attended the AI Engineer Singapore workshops and felt genuinely lucky to secure a spot after being on the waitlist. The first session, “Beyond RAG: Building Agentic Document Workflows with LlamaIndex,” provided valuable insights into the RAG challenges I’ve been contemplating for the past two years. One key takeaway was that issues such as chunking, retrieval quality, reranking, parsing, and evaluation are not isolated to my work; they are industry-wide challenges that we are all actively addressing. I learned that maintaining a reliable RAG prototype in production is even more difficult than building one. Challenges like evaluation gaps, retrieval drift, and documents that disrupt parsers in unexpected ways add complexity to our efforts. It was incredibly reassuring to connect with others in the room who were grappling with similar questions. Thank you, @Pierre-Loïc Doulcet, for a session that was both practical and thought-provoking. And thank you, @Sherry Jiang, for opening the waitlist and keeping us updated so quickly. #AIEngineering #RAG #LlamaIndex #AIEngineerSG

# AI Engineer Singapore Workshop Insights on RAG Challenges

This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

Days 2 & 3 at AI Engineer Singapore 🧠 

The teams shipping reliable agents aren't using better models. They're doing better engineering.

Notes from sessions by NanoCo (creators of NanoClaw), Daytona, Stripe, Airfoil, Google, Greptile, Z.ai, Figma, Arize AI, adaption, and more:

1. LLMs are non-deterministic and therefore unsafe by design.
Evals, classifiers, and human-in-the-loop all reduce risk — they don't eliminate it. The last line of defense is always environment isolation. Contain the blast radius. Assume the agent will eventually do something wrong.

2. Productivity gains from AI have exposed a new set of bottlenecks.
Human collaboration, human attention, prompt injection, feature bloat. The constraint is no longer what the model can do. It's everything around it.

3. Long-horizon tasks fail from goal drift, not token limits. — Z. ai
3 failure modes: goal drift, error accumulation, inability to pivot. Fixes are operational — reread the goal every N steps, verify after each meaningful action, ask the agent whether to continue or abandon. Benchmark to watch: FrontierSWE.

4. 27.6% of PRs are now AI-generated. — Greptile
AI scores better than humans on revert rate, worse on maintainability. Humans and AI reviews serve different purposes. The less obvious risk: PR descriptions are now a prompt injection surface. Code validation needs to scale with agent output volume.

5. Stripe Minions: AI Agents targeted at small feature requests / code changes. 65% of agent PRs approved in one shot.
One dev box per agent. No shared environments.

6. Good design cannot be trained on outcomes.
Phil Hedayatnia (Airfoil) and Josh Newton (Microsoft) made the same point from different angles: pattern matching is not the same as going through the creative process. Because generation is cheap, the new trap is shipping everything you can build instead of only what you should. Craft and restraint are the new differentiators.

7. Scaling model weights is hitting a ceiling - Sara Hooker (Adaption)
More weights = disproportionate compute cost relative to intelligence gains. The era of adaptation is here: synthetic data + self-improving models + adaptive interfaces. The question is no longer who has the best foundation model. It's who adapts fastest.

8. An underexplored question: where is enterprise adoption actually heading in SEA?
On the ground in Singapore, aggressive enterprise AI demand wasn't the dominant story. The gap between what's being built and what enterprises in SG are buying felt wider than I originally expected. Worth watching.

More refined posts are coming next week.

posts.text:
Good fun this past week learning about the state of AI development and security across a few events (and countries):

Tuesday - Lorikeet presenting their internal agent that lets their GTM team sandbox a version of their product for prospects before the first call, with zero engineering support.

Wed/Thu - AWS Summit Sydney. Deep dive on integrating AI into existing software without touching legacy code. Routing requests to AgentCore for guardrails, identity restriction, and access to most foundation models in a single service.

Fri-Sun - AI Engineer Singapore, hosted by the event goats 🥃 Agrim Singh & Sherry Jiang. Singapore Airlines owes you commission by now.

Favourite talks, in no particular order:
- Vedran Jukic from Daytona sharing how companies should stop trying to make agents unhackable and instead give them free rein in a sandbox with explicit network control and proxied access to sensitive credentials
- Vercel proving why it's the go-to platform for hosting agents on web apps with a sneak peek from Jimmy Lai & JJ Kasper on their upcoming releases
- Ben Guo and the creation of Zo Computer as a way to break away from internet feudalism by running micro SaaS in a personal Linux VM
- Josh Newton from Microsoft's design team sharing tips on how to keep ownership of the creative process when building software, using his app Orbit as a case study
- IBM's work in the open source community and sharing how to build agent harnesses from first principles as well as why they’re needed for reliable outputs courtesy of Tejas Kumar

That’ll do me for a few months.

Just wrapped up 2nd day at AI Engineer event at Singapore. What a fantastic line up, atmosphere, speakers and attendees. Fantastic job 65labs 🙌 👏👏👏 Here's what stuck: Software factories are the future, and they're agentic. Cursor talk reminded me of the digital factories we built in retail 10 years ago during the first wave of digital transformation. Same idea, new tools. Engineers become managers. Agents run the floor. The factory has boilerplate patterns the model knows, guardrails (rules, hooks, tests), and enablers (skills, MCP servers, dev environments). Done right, it's a Michelin kitchen with the human in the loop on what matters. Most forward orgs will run "dark software factories" by end of year. Software is the main user of software now. Vercel Jimmy Lai made this real. When was the last time you opened a docs site? Exactly. Your README, PRs, error messages, playbooks are all execution fuel for agents. One stale example used to mislead one engineer. Now it misleads hundreds of thousands of agent runs before anyone notices. Fix your wikis. Fix your docs. It's infrastructure now. Building is cheap. Owning is expensive. You can ship any feature in an hour. So can your competitor. The question stopped being "can we build this" and became "should this exist, and are we willing to own it for two years?" The edge is deciding what NOT to build. Design for the deciding, not the decision. Google's framing was the best for product people Annie L...Utility tasks want speed. Subjective decisions need comparison, contrast, room to discover. Prompt injection is not a bug. It's the technology. You cannot fully prevent it. A real sandbox keeps secrets outside the agent, proxies network through an allow-list, logs every command, logs every prompt and response. If your agent reads the internet and you don't have this, you're one PDF away from a bad day. Daytona AI agents make different bugs, not fewer. Your validation has to scale to how the bots fail, not how humans fail. Exa conrad soon showcased interesting use cases for when you're building search for agents - not humans. Agents have different needs, so design with this in mind. Lots of use cases for commerce and retail to explore. Louis Walsh Scarcity is gone. So are the systems built on it. Quarterly roadmaps, 30 ideas filtered down to 3, programme managers wrangling priorities. All of it comes from a world where building was slow and expensive. That world is gone. Build all 30, eval them, keep the 3 that worked, revert the rest. The moat moves from code to brand, GTM, data, and judgement. Max Buckley Hard work moved from execution to judgement. Faster code, much higher bar on what to build, what to own, how to validate. Shift to builder and IC is clear. + my vibe coded gamified conference map pokemon style with battle and collection screens.

posts.text: There are stalwarts from Silicon Valley who are reputed AI builders and techies and then there are sponsored students from institutes like ITE at AI Engineer Singapore event today! This is an absolute example of inclusivity at Singapore's AI builder's community driven by 65labs lead by 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang and team. Ever since I learnt about AI Engineer I have been following closely and learning from the community. It gives me hope that there's so much potential for AI development in Singapore. No conference has impressed me in all these years as this community led event. Proves that ground up initiatives have an entirely different Aura that draws audience. They have succeeded in bring almost the entire SF community of leading AI builders to Singapore today. Go check on x.com yourself to see their tweets. I would recommend Singapore Tourism Board board to consider giving them an award for best attraction of the year 2026 😆 Really excited to share that I've been selected as one of 20 students to receive a fully sponsored ticket to attend AI Engineer Singapore, happening from 15–17 May! Can't wait to be in the same room as the people actually shaping where AI in software, design, and robotics is headed, and to hear firsthand how they're thinking about what comes next. Really grateful to 65labs for organising AI Engineer Singapore, and to Rachael De Foe, Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Ainul Md Razib, Patrick Kelly, Neil Chang, Hsu Ken Ooi, Ivan Leo, Kaspar Hidayat, Zayne Zhang, and to everyone else who sponsored the student tickets and made this possible! If you're going to be at the event, I'd love to connect!

Had a great weekend at AI Engineer Singapore 🇸🇬

Loved the workshops, talks and conversations with others during the event. Came away with lots of new ideas, perspectives and things I can’t wait to build with!

Huge thank you to the incredible team 65labs for putting together such an amazing event! Really appreciate all the effort that went into it.

#AIEngineer #AIEngineerSingapore

Hrishi fit 18 months of data work into 10 minutes at AI Engineer Singapore - and believe me, that was some lossless compression. 

Some well-loved zingers: 
>It's only in code that really legacy is a bad word.
>The merge-cell button in Excel was one of the greatest crimes against humanity
>Be a goldfish. It's good. (and that one angler fish)
>The online and offline meme (yes, as dramatic as the meme)
>The kitten who dreamt of pipelines

Here's a longer, interactive version: https://lnkd.in/geZA5WJA

Huge thanks to 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Kaspar Hidayat Daren T. Ivan Leo swyx and everyone who came up after to talk to us about Hankweave, long-horizon agents, and their data traumas 😃

Spent the past few days after attending AI Engineer Singapore experimenting with an idea that kept sticking with me: What if regulations could move beyond PDFs and become executable workflows?

I used Cursor to put together a new version of my personal project RegLens. Compared with an earlier version focused more on analysis and summarization, this version tries to move closer toward execution:
→ materiality assessment
→ executive briefing
→ accountable workstreams
→ operational execution plans
→ traceable verification logic

One thing that stood out while building it: trust, consistency and understanding why something matters to a specific company turned out to be harder (and more interesting) than simply extracting obligations from a document.

Huge thanks to everyone who shared ideas and feedback during AI Engineer SG. Particularly appreciate the discussions and inputs from:
Cursor (Nick Miller and Jack), Arize AI (Sean and Fuad), LlamaIndex (Pierre-Loic) and Convex (Michael)

Also a big thank you to the AI Engineer SG organizers: Sherry 🥃 Agrim Rachael 🇸🇬 Yong Quan and rest of the 65labs crew
Still lots left to improve, but learned a lot through the process.

There were many interesting teams and products at the event, but a few that stayed top of mind from presentations, meetup sessions, booths and conversations were Exa, Zo Computer, Magic Patterns, Resaro and Airfoil

AI Engineer Singapore — Day 2 completed! 🚀 I was genuinely amazed by the crowd, energy, and orchestration behind such a huge event. Big thank you to 65labs, Sherry Jiang , and 🥃 Agrim Singh for bringing AI Engineer to Singapore and creating such a strong space for the AI builder community here. 🙌 One of the biggest themes today was clear: agents are moving from side experiments into real engineering workflows. 🤖 Agents are becoming real engineering teammates From coding agents to autonomous workflows, the focus is shifting from “AI as assistant” to AI systems that can triage, review, test, and execute tasks with proper guardrails. It feels like AI-powered PR reviewers are becoming more common — not just to speed up code review, but also to help teams catch issues earlier, validate changes, and improve engineering productivity. 🔐 Security and isolation matter more than ever As agents gain access to tools, files, browsers, terminals, and credentials, sandboxing, zero-trust design, and human-in-the-loop approval are becoming critical. The more powerful agents become, the more important it is to design safe boundaries around what they can access, execute, and approve. I also had the chance to attend the Vercel community evening with the Next.js team, where they shared what’s new in Next.js for the age of AI and agents. It was especially exciting to meet Jimmy Lai , in person and hear more about how Vercel is thinking about the future of building on the web. Big thanks to the Vercel team for showcasing their products, sharing their insights, and taking the time to explain what is coming next. Can’t wait for the final day! 🚀 #AIEngineer #AIEngineering #Agents #CodingAgents #Nextjs #Vercel #SoftwareEngineering #GenerativeAI #SingaporeTech

posts.text:
1,000 people. 3 months. A collective called 65 Labs just shipped the highest-signal AI event in Singapore to date. 

AI Engineer Singapore wrapped yesterday.

Brain full. Cup empty. Best problem to have.

Here's what I'm taking away:

The moat moved from the model to the harness.

Every serious operator on stage spent their slot describing what sits ABOVE the model: orchestration, evals, sandboxes, MCP gateways, approval loops, identity layers, skills.

Frontier model training is a $10B game played in San Francisco and Hangzhou.

Deployment infrastructure at sovereign scale is what Singapore is building.

GovTech is wiring up a harness for 150,000 public officers. Cognition picked SG as their Asia HQ. Featherless routes 30,000 open models from here. The Foreign Minister opened day one demoing an agent he built on a Raspberry Pi.

This isn't catch-up. It's a different bet.

Singapore is going to be the country that figures out how to deploy AI inside institutions, at a depth nobody else has tried.

And it'll ship before anyone notices.

Carrying all of this with me to Australia next month.

Big thanks to 65labs, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, for the invite to come along and lend a hand, and a humble bow to Brian C., Yee Ming T. for running the day to day operations with the team.

If you were there, drop the moment that stuck with you. Or just connect.

posts.text:
Singapore's Foreign Minister built an AI second brain on a Raspberry Pi in his evenings.

At AI Engineer Singapore, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked through the "Second Brain" he built for his diplomatic work — and what makes it so inspiring is that his day job has nothing to do with tech or AI. Yet there he was, showing a room of engineers his architecture and workflow 

His line stuck with me: "The barriers have collapsed." He's right — five years ago, what he built would have needed a team and a substantial budget.

But the part every aspiring AI builder should hear is what came next: "I did not write Claude. I did not write whisper.cpp or the other tools. I wrote the glue." That's the whole game now. 

The human role has shifted — AI is powerful enough that your job isn't to build every part. It's to start with a problem or an idea, then act as the orchestrator: spotting what the workflow needs, picking the best tool for each job, and assembling them into an outcome.

So when people ask me the best way to pick up AI, my answer is simple. It's to learn by doing, ideally with guidance from an experienced practitioner. If a Foreign Minister can assemble one in his evenings, the barrier was never the technology. It was starting.

#AIEngineerSingapore #LearnByDoing #AITransformation #SingaporeTech #aidotengineer

posts.text: So I've been somewhat working behind the scenes, but I'm organising the AI Engineer Singapore conference this May (in less than 3 weeks!). If you've been around some of the 65labs builder events in Singapore over the past year, AIE Singapore will feel like a natural next step. It is really a continuation of that same energy that we've been deliberately crafting, creating more spaces for people to come together, learn, and build alongside one another. What's been an interesting reflection for me as I wrangle through the scale of the event is \*why\* we keep doing this. Every single person on the core team is doing this on top of a full-time job. No one has to be here. But we keep showing up because we genuinely care about building this community and we've seen firsthand the appetite for more opportunities like this. This conference is really just us taking everything we've been doing, and making it even bigger. Honestly, the response has been kind of incredible. We're bringing together a lineup of speakers that we're genuinely excited about. Folks like Ryo Lu (Head of Design at Cursor, also one of the early people at Notion!), Tibo (leading Codex at OpenAI), Sara Hooker (Co-Founder at Adaption Labs), all alongside engineers, designers, and operators who are shaping how this space evolves. We’re also backed by partners we really respect, including OpenAI, z.ai, Google DeepMind, Cursor, Arize, Cloudflare, Govtech, the list is so long!!! It still feels incredibly surreal, but also speaks to the trust that’s been built through all the smaller things that came before this. And as though planning a conference as a passion project isn't insane enough, we've also been running a series of Road to AIE events as a leadup, all designed to keep that same spirit of experimentation and connection going. (If you're interested, we have a Luma page with all the upcoming events: https://luma.com/1eofvp02) On a personal note, it’s been really fun for me to come in and take the reins on logistics for this. It’s a bit chaotic behind the scenes, but this is exactly the kind of chaos my brain enjoys, taking a lot of moving pieces and bringing them into something that (hopefully) feels seamless on the day. More than anything, I’m just really excited to see this come together. If the past few months are anything to go by, it’s going to be a room full of people who are curious, generous, and building in interesting ways. Quick thank you to Sherry, 🥃 Agrim, Ivan, Kaspar and Rachael for trusting me and bringing me into this!!! (Even though it means I'm breathing down your neck for deliverables every single day...) If this sounds like your kind of space, we would love to have you there! Wave 2 tickets close April 30th: https://lnkd.in/gZNFqdCj. It'll be worth it ;) everyone needs an adlin in their lives! love that you're in the chaos with us!! <3 Adlin is world class taskmaster someone has to crack the whip lol Hi adlin, Really inspiring opportunity! I’m actively working on GenAI and AI engineering projects and would love to explore how students or early researchers can contribute to initiatives like this. Would it be alright if I connected to learn more? Nicely done, Adlin Zainal! Looking forward to hearing amazing feedback about this conference!

posts.text: I am incredibly excited to announce that I’ll be taking the stage at AI Engineer Singapore 2026 this May! 🇸🇬✨ Generative AI initially promised a massive relief for scaling digital content. However, we all know the reality: standard models often struggle with complex design parameters, frequently spitting out inconsistent pixel arrangements rather than the clean, scalable, flat design vector outputs that enterprises actually need (and also, not on-brand!) In my session - "Beyond Flat Design Output and Autocomplete: Solving the Complex Design Problems and Enterprise Design Bottleneck with AI" - we are going to explore how agentic AI fundamentally resolves this historical bottleneck by moving beyond mere prompt-based "autocomplete" or complicated, heavily manual tools-based editors into true autonomous, goal-oriented and brand-specific execution. I’ll be sharing a candid look at how we are actively solving this at Obello, and I couldn't be prouder of the systems we are building alongside Ben Pham, Ollie Ralph, Tony T., and the rest of our brilliant team. Ultimately, our goal isn't to replace designers, but to elevate human designers back to their rightful role as strategic champions, rather than repetitive pixel-pushers. 📅 Date: May 15–17, 2026 📍 Location: The Capitol Theatre Singapore If you are an engineer, founder, designer, or operator looking to have sharper conversations about what it actually takes to build with AI, this is the conference to attend. Missed AI Engineer Singapore in person, which makes me even more grateful that Dr Vivian Balakrishnan's session got uploaded to YouTube. I've always seen him as an astute and charismatic person. What I didn't expect was this side of him: a builder, a tinkerer, a learner by doing. Couldn't agree more with this methodlogy. A few quotes that stayed with me: "𝒀𝒐𝒖 𝒄𝒂𝒏𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒈𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒏 𝒂 𝒕𝒆𝒄𝒉𝒏𝒐𝒍𝒐𝒈𝒚 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒉𝒂𝒗𝒆 𝒐𝒏𝒍𝒚 𝒃𝒆𝒆𝒏 𝒃𝒓𝒊𝒆𝒇𝒆𝒅 𝒐𝒏." Get your hands dirty if you actually want to grasp and govern technology for our good, instead of the other way round. This rings true for me — building ChickenDuck, and even becoming a Cohere Solutions Architect. • It's about remaining curious • It's about having an intrepid spirit, being unafraid of things foreign to us • It's about deriving joy in the process I've learnt to cut down on my grand master planning and just get down to business. Still working on that. Slowly but surely, the unknown becomes known. "𝑾𝒆 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒑𝒆𝒓𝒉𝒂𝒑𝒔 𝒐𝒏𝒆 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒎𝒐𝒔𝒕 𝒑𝒓𝒊𝒗𝒊𝒍𝒆𝒈𝒆𝒅 𝒈𝒆𝒏𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒕𝒐 𝒃𝒆 𝒍𝒊𝒗𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒕𝒉𝒓𝒐𝒖𝒈𝒉 𝒂 𝒓𝒆𝒗𝒐𝒍𝒖𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏." Team Human Race here. We get to steward it, not just survive it. Truly, what a time to be alive. "𝑺𝒊𝒏𝒈𝒂𝒑𝒐𝒓𝒆 𝒊𝒔 𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒍𝒊𝒌𝒆𝒍𝒚 𝒕𝒐 𝒃𝒆 𝒂𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒇𝒓𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒆𝒓 𝒐𝒇 𝒎𝒐𝒅𝒆𝒍 𝒅𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒍𝒐𝒑𝒎𝒆𝒏𝒕, 𝒃𝒖𝒕 𝒘𝒆 𝒄𝒂𝒏 𝒃𝒆 𝒂𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒇𝒓𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒆𝒓 𝒐𝒇 𝒅𝒆𝒑𝒍𝒐𝒚𝒎𝒆𝒏𝒕 𝒂𝒕 𝒔𝒄𝒂𝒍𝒆." "𝑹𝒆𝒂𝒍 𝒗𝒂𝒍𝒖𝒆 𝒊𝒔 𝒄𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒕𝒆𝒅 𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒏 𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒚𝒐𝒏𝒆 — 𝒕𝒆𝒂𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒔, 𝒕𝒆𝒄𝒉𝒏𝒊𝒄𝒊𝒂𝒏𝒔, 𝒎𝒂𝒏𝒂𝒈𝒆𝒓𝒔, 𝒆𝒏𝒈𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒆𝒓𝒔, 𝒅𝒐𝒄𝒕𝒐𝒓𝒔, 𝒍𝒂𝒘𝒚𝒆𝒓𝒔, 𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒏 𝒎𝒊𝒏𝒊𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒓𝒔 — 𝒘𝒉𝒐 𝒖𝒏𝒅𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒊𝒓 𝒘𝒐𝒓𝒌, 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒗𝒊𝒅𝒆𝒅 𝒘𝒊𝒕𝒉 𝑨𝑰 𝒕𝒐𝒐𝒍𝒔 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒕𝒓𝒂𝒏𝒔𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒎 𝒉𝒐𝒘 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒚 𝒈𝒆𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒋𝒐𝒃 𝒅𝒐𝒏𝒆; 𝒐𝒓 𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒏 𝒃𝒆𝒕𝒕𝒆𝒓, 𝒓𝒆-𝒆𝒏𝒈𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒆𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒓𝒆 𝒘𝒐𝒓𝒌𝒇𝒍𝒐𝒘." Met Ryo Lu today, Head of Design at Cursor at AI Engineer Singapore. I am a big fan of his way of building software. He pulled out his phone and showed me what he’s been running:

→ A classic Mac environment, fully functional, on mobile

→ An iPod music app with a retro click wheel wired to Apple Music

→ Classic Doom, running clean

→ Local AI agents handling real workflows underneath all of it
Including, apparently, writing and refining today’s keynote.

That’s not a side project. That’s a person who builds their own infrastructure, then uses it for work that actually matters.

Most people talk about code and agentic AI. Ryo just lives in it.

That’s the bar.

Curious mind. Builder mode. 🇸🇬

posts.text:
I walked into an AI hackathon last weekend with zero code experience. There was also a rule: if you touch your laptop, you have to wear a lobster costume. Your AI agent codes. You just direct it.

I am an illustrator. A creative. I've spent over a decade making things with my hands, not terminals. So when I registered for Ralphthon, an AI hackathon run by token maxxing and funded by OpenAI during AI Engineer Singapore [65labs Sherry Jiang and team], I genuinely did not know if I belonged there.

Turns out the thing that mattered most wasn't knowing how to code.

It was knowing how to think. How to write. How to communicate a problem so clearly that an AI agent could run with it.

In one day, I built Cari, an autonomous agent that helps Singapore caregivers find every government grant and subsidy they qualify for, from a single plain-English message AND voice chat*. No jargons. No social worker required.

The room was full of engineers. I felt the impostor syndrome hard. And then I watched my agent pipeline run, and I thought: this is just directed thinking. This is what creatives do.

I made a vlog about the whole experience. What it felt like. What I built. What I'd tell any artist, designer, or writer who thinks the AI space isn't for them.

Just watched Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan's keynote at AI Engineer Singapore, and one line cut through everything else.
"You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on."

Singapore's Foreign Affairs Minister didn't speak about AI from a distance. He built his own tools, NanoClaw and Obsidian, to manage the cognitive load of international diplomacy. His point is uncomfortable for most leaders: reading summaries is not enough. You have to get your hands dirty.

Three things stayed with me.
First, real AI value is created at the ground level, not in data centers. The economic payoff lands when a lawyer, doctor, teacher, or contact center agent re-engineers their daily workflow with bespoke tools. Not when an enterprise deploys a frontier model and calls it transformation.

Second, not every problem needs an LLM. Dr. Balakrishnan's warning against treating large language models as a universal hammer is one that the CX industry badly needs to hear. Deterministic, rule-based systems still have a critical role. The future is hybrid, likely neuro-symbolic, and far more energy-efficient than what we're building today.

Third, and most importantly, accountability cannot be outsourced. Computation, storage, and knowledge retrieval are all delegable. But personal understanding and the consequences of decisions made on your watch? Those stay with you.

Singapore's AI strategy is built on deployment at scale, not foundational model supremacy. That's a smart, honest bet for a small nation. It's also the right framing for most enterprises.

Last weekend at the AI Engineer Hackathon, together with Yan Rui Tan, we built something called Sonic Intelligence 🎧.

The project started from a thought that kept bothering us:

AI can see. 
AI can read. 
But most systems still barely listen.

And I don’t mean speech-to-text.

I mean understanding environments through sound.

A sudden silence in a noisy room. 
Footsteps approaching from behind. 
The difference between a normal machine hum and something failing. 
The emotional tone behind voices. 
Patterns humans instinctively notice without thinking.

Audio carries an insane amount of information, but compared to vision and text, it still feels underexplored in AI.

So during the hackathon, we decided to experiment with building a system around real-time audio intelligence:
🔊 environmental awareness 
🧠 contextual sound understanding 
⚡ live multimodal reasoning 
🤖 intelligent audio-driven pipelines 

One funny thing about hackathons is how your mental state evolves over time 😂

Hour 1: 
“This idea could actually be huge.”

Hour 5: 
“Why is dependency management destroying us?”

Hour 9: 
“Wait… IT WORKS.”

Unfortunately, we didn’t manage to present the project in time during the presentation slot 😭 
But honestly, we still learned a lot throughout the process, met many amazing builders, and had a really fun time pushing the idea as far as we could within the hackathon timeline. And it was funny watching AI agents debating over the topic we gave them.

One thing I noticed this time:
The AI space is shifting away from isolated single-input systems.

The future feels increasingly:
- multimodal
- real-time
- agentic
- environment-aware

Not just AI that responds to prompts…
but AI that continuously interprets the world around it.

posts.text: Singapore’s Foreign Minister Built His Own AI Second Brain on a Raspberry Pi. Here’s Why Every Leader Should Do the Same. In his keynote at AI Engineer Singapore, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan didn’t deliver abstract vision. He shared the architecture, constraints, and hard-won lessons from deploying NanoClaw, a self-hosted Claude agent running 24/7 as his “second brain” for diplomacy. It connects WhatsApp/Telegram for chat-based prep, ingests speeches and briefings, builds a compounding knowledge graph (inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Wiki), transcribes voice notes locally, and delivers persistent, contextual intelligence. All on modest hardware. All under his control. Key takeaway from the man responsible for Singapore’s foreign policy: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.” This isn’t hype. It’s a direct challenge to every CEO, founder, minister, and policymaker still consuming AI via executive summaries and vendor demos. Reality check: • Token subsidies from labs won’t last. Compute and power costs are rising. • Stateless chatbots hit walls fast for serious work. • Memory, tools, and tight integration separate toys from infrastructure. • The real moat is your data + your workflows, not the base model. Balakrishnan learned this by doing exactly as he urges others. Barriers to entry have collapsed. A sitting minister found time to assemble this. What’s stopping you? Call to companies and entrepreneurs: Stop piloting. Mandate hands-on building. Give your best people Raspberry Pis (or equivalent), open-source stacks like NanoClaw, and time to integrate AI into core operations. The productivity gap will widen between renters of intelligence and owners of memory systems. To leaders of countries: Educate and deploy at scale. Integrate agentic AI into government workflows, schools, and national infrastructure by building and iterating, not regulating from ignorance. Singapore is demonstrating the path: pragmatic, hands-on, sovereign capability. This isn’t about coding from scratch. It’s tool assembly, workflow ownership, and closing the loop between human expertise and AI augmentation. The diplomat (or executive) who learns to work with these systems gains a decisive edge today. Dr Balakrishnan’s gist is public. The talk is available. The hardware is cheap. What are you building this week? Persistent memory systems outperform stateless models for complex workflows because they retain context and learn continuously. RAI AI demonstrates this by enabling customized data analysis across specific tags, locations, and timeframes instead of delivering generic results that ignore your operational nuances.

Inspired by Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs in a recent talk on “Building a ‘Second Brain’: Opportunities, Risks, and Implications for AI Adoption in Singapore,” I was reminded of the importance of practical experience, deliberate practice, and continuous application over theory alone.

On a lighter note, there was also a point about how almost everything can be outsourced, but not your understanding and accountability. It echoes a thought I’ve often had: in a globalised world where import, export, and outsourcing are normal, what remains truly non-transferable is your own heart, mind, and discipline.

The key takeaway for me is simple but powerful: learning is not passive. It is built through doing, refining, failing, and repeating with intent.
I’ve summarised the speech using NotebookLM for my own learning and motivation, and I’m sharing this to encourage others to stay consistent with their goals, whether things are going smoothly or not.

If anything is missing or misinterpreted in my summary, I sincerely apologise. The full context and depth can be better appreciated through the original YouTube video linked below.

posts.text:
Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Vivian Balakrishnan runs his second brain on a Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM.

He showed the whole stack at the AI Engineer Summit last week, walking through it for twenty minutes without a single slide on theory. NanoClaw with Baileys handling his WhatsApp  comms, Mnemon for graph memory, Ollama  running embeddings locally, Whisper for voice capture, Obsidian sitting on top as the wiki layer. He built it himself, on hardware that costs less than a business class lunch in Changi, and he uses it every day to think.

The line that has stayed with me since: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.”

That sentence describes the gap I see in almost every executive conversation across APJ right now, where leaders are commissioning AI strategies they have never personally used the underlying tools to build, signing off on operating models they could not describe at the level of a single workflow if asked to. The briefing deck has quietly replaced the hands-on hour, and most boards seem comfortable with that trade.

Balakrishnan’s argument is not that every executive should learn to deploy containers. His point is that direct contact with the technology has become part of the governance job, because without it the risk frameworks turn into performance and the operating model design stays one full layer abstracted from the thing it is meant to govern.

If a sitting Foreign Minister can find the time to run Ollama and Mnemon on a Pi in his own kitchen, the question for the rest of us is no longer about capacity. It is about willingness to do the work ourselves, on cheap hardware, in the evenings, until we actually understand what we are accountable for.

AI Engineer Singapore. The energy in the room. The cracked engineers. The people moving the needle. The people building. I can’t fully put it into words, but once you see it, you know the ceiling is much higher than what you thought. Here are some of my takeaways: 1. You can’t govern a technology you have only been briefed on That was probably one of the most prominent takeaways from Dr Vivian Balakrishnan’s speech. Because it is fundamentally true. You can’t strategize effectively around something you don’t understand. You can’t decide where to take your product next if you don’t know what the technology is good at, where it breaks, and what it makes possible. And this is not just about using ChatGPT and attaching a few MCP connectors. It is about building. Because when you build, you understand how agents actually work underneath the hood. 2. Ground-up value creation Another point that stood out was the idea of ground-up value creation. Real AI impact does not happen only through top-down strategy. It happens when people start applying AI to real problems in their own work. Individual by individual. Workflow by workflow. Team by team. Broad AI strategy matters, but the real test is whether the use of AI creates better experiences, improves outcomes, and delivers real value to end users. 3. This is the era of builders If you have an idea, ship it. If you see a user problem, build for it. There’s a phrase: “Ideas are cheap, execution is everything.” Guess what? Execution on building products has become cheaper too. The cost of going from idea to prototype has collapsed. The tools are better. The feedback loops are shorter. The barrier to building is lower. You no longer need a huge team or months of planning just to test whether something can work. Tiny teams can now build, ship, and iterate at a speed that used to be impossible. That means the advantage now goes to people who are willing to build, test, learn, and iterate quickly. And as the quote goes: “The best way to predict the future is to create it.” So what’s stopping us? 4. Spectrum of AI literacy There is a spectrum of AI literacy across and outside the industry. Some people are not using the tools because of skepticism. Some people only know AI as ChatGPT. And some people are driving the progress of these tools on a day-to-day basis. Even within the AI industry, there is a huge disparity. There are people wiring up a few tools and calling it an agent. There are people who fundamentally understand how agents, harnesses, tools, and skills work. And then there is a whole other level: the people in frontier labs pushing the industry forward. posts.text:
Two days into AI Engineer Singapore, the strongest signal is not “use more agents.”

It is this: Most teams are not ready for agents yet.

Not because the models are weak. Because the factory around the model is weak.

I kept hearing the same idea from different angles.

Daytona session was about infrastructure for agents: sandboxes, security, model choice, context recycling, and the danger of letting vendors own the layer your agents run on.

Exa workshop showed search becoming structured context for agents. Not search results for humans. Search results as markdown, rendered outputs, PDFs, and reliable inputs that agents can consume.

Cursor “agent factory” framing hit the hardest for me: the factory is harder to build than the product.

You need specs. Skills. READMEs. Test environments. Clear phases. Parallel tasks. Sequential tasks. PR review loops. Agents that can complain when the workflow is bad.

If the agent goes off the rails, that is not only an agent problem. It is a factory problem.

The OpenAI Codex pointed in the same direction: explicitly spawn subagents, use skills, turn memory on, use docs, create hooks, and give the agent a better operating environment.

One thing felt almost universally accepted: the human is no longer needed to type most of the code.

That does not remove the human from the process. It moves the human upstream.

The work shifts from writing every line to designing the system where agents can write, test, fail, recover, and ship safely.

My takeaway: the next advantage is not having an agent. Everyone will have agents.

The advantage is having a system where agents can actually work.

Context. Sandboxes. Tests. Permissions. Memory. Specs. Observability. Human checkpoints.

This is why I’m becoming more interested in software factories than coding agents.

A coding agent is useful. A software factory can change how a whole team builds.

Are you building one? Drop a comment.

Honestly, I've been busy building a knowledge base so that when the right agentic tool comes along, I'll plug and play. It's been too costly to run OpenClaw for myself while paying for Codex/Claude/Cursor and other tools on a monthly basis to build other things. But looking back, Vibe coding since Sept '25 has brought me to a place I never expected myself to be in.

AI Engineer Singapore가 오늘 마무리되었습니다. 직접 듣지는 못했지만 개인적으로 이번 행사에서 가장 인상깊었던 장면은 바로 싱가포르 외교부장관 비비안 발라크리쉬난 박사의 발표였던 것 같습니다. 

정부에 몸담고 있으면서 직접 NanoClaw를 써서 Raspberry Pi에 개인비서 에이전트를 구축한 이야기는 여러모로 시사하는 바가 많은 것 같습니다. 젠슨 황, 데미스 하사비스, 다리오 아모데이 등 대부분의 리더들이 오래전부터 AI 규제의 필요성을 이야기했지만 실제로 규제를 만드는 입법부와 규제를 실행하는 정부쪽의 움직임은 잘 포착이 되지 않아왔습니다. 

비비안 장관은 이렇게 말했다고 합니다. "우리가 잘 모르는 것을 제대로 규제할 수 있겠느냐" 제 개인적으로는 정말 사막에서 오아시스를 만난 것 같이 반가운 말이었습니다. 전문가를 불러서 이야기를 듣는 데서 멈추지 않고 직접 손을 움직여서 뭔가를 만들어본 리더라면, 어디까지가 실제 현재 기술로 가능하고 어디까지가 마케팅을 위해 과장되었는지 구분할 수 있을 것이기 때문입니다.

지난 2024년 12월 젠슨 황 Nvidia CEO가 한 인터뷰에서 "정부는 단순히 규제만을 강제하는 게 아니라 직접 AI를 사용하는 사용자가 되어야 한다"고 말한 바 있는데, 2026년 5월 싱가포르에서 이렇게 현실이 되었네요. 이번 비비안 박사의 발표를 계기로 앞으로 더 많은 시도와 배움이 공공분야에서 보이면 참 좋겠다는 바람을 가져봅니다.

You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.
That was the key message.

At AI Engineer Singapore, Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan shared how he uses NanoClaw to communicate with his AI assistant through WhatsApp.

The point was not novelty.

It was cognitive overload.

He said that in one month, he was visiting 12 countries, meeting hundreds of people, and needing to understand each country’s economy, geography, culture, history, conflicts and personalities.

That is where AI becomes interesting.

Not as a chatbot.

But as a working memory system.

A second brain that helps organise information, retrieve context, and support real work.

AI literacy is no longer just knowing how to prompt.

It is understanding how agents, memory, workflows and governance come together.

You need to understand what it feels like when the tool becomes part of the work.

You need to experience how it changes the work itself.

What a weekend, feel super energised after AI Engineer Singapore event this weekend. Thank you Rachael De Foe, Sherry Jiang and the 65labs team for this inspiring event. 🙌 🙌 Main highlights from the last 3 days: 

AI as a creative collaborator, not a replacement The "magic pencil" mindset: AI speeds iteration, but taste and craft stay human-led. Raising the floor doesn't automatically raise the ceiling.

Agents are tools in a loop, not magic Coding agents = agent loop + bash/runtime. It is all about how you structure, extend, and add guardrails.

AI with personality, not just capability, a reminder that scaling intelligence isn't the only axis. Building character, opinion, and proactive behavior into agents opens a different design space.

The macro shift: knowledge scarcity → knowledge abundance AI-native companies vs. incumbents on multi-year transformation curves. Roles aren't being backfilled. Smaller teams are moving faster. Hiring bar is shifting toward AI fundamentals — tool calls, model basics, inference thinking — not surface-level usage.

Production reliability comes from decomposition The pattern from Google DeepMind that resonated most: Routing → Transform → Generate → Safety check. Break systems into deterministic steps rather than one giant prompt. And many more...

Biggest highlight was also for my 4 year old to see and interact with Robot from The Robot Company and learn all about how to build a robot, and watch robot painting.
