"𝑌𝑜𝑢 𝑐𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑔𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑛 𝑎 𝑡𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑛𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑦 𝑡ℎ𝑎𝑡 𝑦𝑜𝑢 ℎ𝑎𝑣𝑒 𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑦 𝑏𝑒𝑒𝑛 𝑏𝑟𝑖𝑒𝑓𝑒𝑑 𝑜𝑛."

That was the closing line that Claude wrote for Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr Vivian Balakrishnan during his opening speech at AI Engineer Singapore. He spoke about how he built his own open-source "second brain" using NanoClaw to manage information. 

True mastery requires getting your hands dirty. This resonated deeply because I have been spending the last couple of weeks doing that: building my first Telegram bot for family management.

Here are the three major takeaways:

𝟏) 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝
You can delegate tasks and computation to AI, but you cannot outsource your own conceptual understanding. AI didn't replace my learning, but accelerated it. I still had to understand what I was building and troubleshoot when things broke.

𝟐) 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥
Macro policies are essential, but the true payoff happens workflow by workflow. It is driven by ordinary professionals re-engineering their daily routines. AI gives non-technical people the tools and confidence to build something real right now.

𝟑) 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐠
The essential tools have already been invented. This is the future of lifelong learning, where we don't just attend formal courses, but active, AI-assisted experimentation.

The barriers to entry have collapsed. The future belongs to the builders and practitioners who are willing to look stupid, ask questions, and create. What are you building today?

#AI #LifelongLearning #Singapore

I used AI to plan it. AI to build it. And shipped a product about how AI should adapt to humans.

Solo. 7 hours. AI Engineer Hackathon, Singapore.
This is Cadence. ↓

The problem: 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁. 𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝟵 𝗔𝗠 𝗱𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗹𝗲𝗽𝘁 𝟴 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗿 𝟰. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸 𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗸𝗶𝗱 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗻𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁.

The science says otherwise. Cognitive capacity fluctuates with sleep debt, hormonal cycles, and training load. Yet no planner accounts for any of it.
Cadence does.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝗻 — 𝘀𝗹𝗲𝗲𝗽, 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆, 𝗰𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 (𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝟲 𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗿-𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀) 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘆. 𝗘𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗟𝗮𝗯𝘀 𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹 𝗶𝘁.

𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀. 𝗥𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗲. 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿.

posts.text:
Ministers in Governments all over the world, will now be able to let the public see ALL of their decisions and activities, thanks to this new Sovereign AI technology 🔥

Singapore’s Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan just did something no sitting minister has ever done…

He published the source code of the AI assistant he built and uses every day. 

It runs on a Raspberry Pi, hooks into his WhatsApp and Gmail, transcribes his voice notes, drafts his speeches, and gets smarter over time.  

He calls it his “second brain for a diplomat.” 

His words: “You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on.” 

and he means it literally.

What makes this remarkable isn’t the technology. It’s the architecture philosophy. Voice notes are transcribed on-device, vector embeddings run locally, and each messaging group gets its own isolated container, meaning no sensitive content ever leaves his network.  

For MPs and ministers, this matters enormously. 

Cloud-based AI tools mean your briefings, policy positions, and constituent conversations sit on someone else’s server. 

A self-hosted, local-first setup gives you the full power of AI with none of the data sovereignty risk…it’s the only model that’s actually fit for public office.

In his own words, “the barriers to entry have come down so dramatically, everyone should embark on their personal experiments” 

he proved it by running this on a Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM that’s at least two years old.  

This isn’t a government moonshot or a million-dollar procurement. 

It’s an accessible, open-source blueprint any MP could replicate this weekend. 

The question isn’t whether AI will reshape governance…in fact, it already is. 

The question is : are your representatives are building it, or just being briefed on it?

[Singaporean Pride, and a Commentary on AI] One of the reasons why I am a proud Singaporean, and want to do my level best to plant the Singapore 🇸🇬 flag globally in my humble way. Singapore is known for good governance. But what makes good governance tick is not flowery language, but understanding what we govern. And understanding what we govern means we must dabble with what we govern. And given how almost every PMET job in Singapore has been disrupted with AI, it means almost every PMET has to understand AI, and to understand AI we have to tinker and gain personal insights through our tinkering. That is what Foreign Minister Dr. Vivian Balakrisnan mentioned at the 65labs AI Engineer conference (I caught the keynote on Youtube, and was unfortunately not at the conference itself). If the Minister can tinker with NanoClaw, understand how containerisation brings security benefit as opposed to OpenClaw, and publicises the project on his own Github, I realised I can do better. 😉 Highly, highly inspirational. Listening to the keynote in full (https://lnkd.in/gHKRQ9Ps) is highly recommended. #AI #walkingthetalk #leadership (Disclaimer: Not AI-drafted. I wanted to write this myself because it is an opportunity to go slow, and think of what I want to write. We should use AI to augment our thinking, and provide refinement, but not replace our personal experiences and accountability; these are the two aspects that AI cannot, and should never replace.)

“You cannot govern a technology you’ve only been briefed on.” This morning, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into a room full of builders and did something that genuinely mattered: …he showed up as one himself He opened up his actual workflow, talked through the second brain he’s been building, the tradeoffs, the implications, the limits, and the things he’s still figuring out. And I’m sure, before he spoke, there were skeptics in the room. Builders have heard enough people talk about technology from a distance to know the difference between someone who has touched the tools and someone who has only read summaries about them. What struck me most wasn’t even the talk itself, it was what happened after He stayed. He went off stage and spent time with young builders. Students. Engineers. People still figuring out their place in all of this. Then he stayed in the room to watch Gavriel Cohen’s creator of NanoClaw talk because he genuinely wanted to hear it. And as someone on the organising team, I can tell you that none of it was staged and all of it was him. That detail will stay with me for a long time. There were students sitting in the front row today who now have a completely different reference point for what leadership can look like. He wasn’t speaking above the work. He was actually doing it. I’m very aware that what happened today was much bigger than us. Thank you, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan. Putting together 65labs AI Engineer has always been rooted in a hope that Singapore can become a place where serious builders collide openly, generously, and ambitiously. Today, you helped us show that it already is.

* +1

My biggest takeaway from the AI Engineer Singapore conference this year:

AI is no longer just about better models. It is becoming a systems design problem.

A few ideas stayed with me:

1. Agents are coming, but agents alone are not the strategy.  
One slide referenced IDC’s estimate of 1.3 billion AI agents by 2028. The real question is not “Can we add agents?” It is “Where do agents create leverage, and where do they add complexity?”

2. Ideas are becoming execution.  
When software becomes faster and cheaper to build, implementation is no longer the main bottleneck. Judgment is. What is worth building? What should be measured? What should be discarded?

3. Removing waste from systems may be a bigger accelerator than AI itself.  
If the workflow is broken, AI may simply accelerate the mess. Clean process design still matters.

4. Stop using the LLM as one giant problem-solver.  
Use LLMs for language, reasoning, classification, and generation. Use deterministic systems for routing, rules, consistency, and compliance.

A production-ready pattern is not one giant prompt. It is input → router → predefined route → structured transformation → generation → safety check → output.

5. Evaluation has to come first.  
Evals are becoming the modern version of test-driven development. Before fine-tuning, prompt optimization, or adding more agents, teams need golden datasets and clear success metrics.

6. Models are incredible, but they are not magic.  
Safety, compliance, observability, redaction, monitoring, release testing, and domain review still need to exist around the model.

7. For subjective decisions, good AI should design for the deciding, not just the decision.  
The first wave of AI removed friction. But for taste, style, identity, travel, shopping, and creative work, some friction is useful. Users need exploration, comparison, and confidence — not just one auto-generated answer.

My final takeaway:

The winning AI products will not simply be the ones with the biggest models or the most agents. They will be the ones that remove real waste, use LLMs where they are strongest, evaluate rigorously, and turn fast execution into disciplined learning.

You can talk about PostHog, or you can build a custom app for the audience, let them generate real data, and watch it flow into the dashboards live. 

Abel Tan and Khalid Sani crusheddd their workshop at AI Engineer Singapore last week - all about how we use Posthog to close the loop between user data and our next features.

Spent the weekend at the “Road to AI Engineers” event in Singapore — and as someone who is definitely not a coder (maybe a nerd, but certainly a CFO), it was genuinely eye-opening.

What struck me most was not the technology itself, but how quickly AI is moving from “interesting tool” to becoming core infrastructure for governments, businesses, and everyday work.

A few standout moments and takeaways:
🔹 Dr Vivian Balakrishnan’s opening address was particularly impactful.
 Hearing how he personally uses AI agents to improve productivity and effectiveness as Singapore’s Foreign Minister made the conversation around AI feel very real and practical — not theoretical. https://lnkd.in/gDKCtrTM
  
🔹 GovTech’s vision was crystal clear:
Singapore aims to become AI-native, not just AI-enabled
Government officers are actively being trained to use AI and agentic workflows
That distinction between enabled and native stayed with me.

🔹 Some interesting sessions and tools:
Nanocloud → reinforced how critical sandboxing and governance are in an AI-first world

My biggest reflections from the event:
1️⃣ AI is absolutely here to stay
 Singapore is investing heavily to bring the entire ecosystem forward — starting with government agencies.

 AI is powerful, but also resource intensive. The focus should be on solving meaningful problems, not building frivolous applications for the sake of hype.
3️⃣ The possibilities are limitless — and so is the disruption
 The long-term impact remains uncertain, but one thing is clear: individuals and organisations that adapt early will have a significant advantage.

AI Threat Intelligence Briefing (May 3–17, 2026)
 - 548 raw items collected → 42 final entries in the newsletter
 - 8 news, 8 vulnerabilities, 10 advisories, 8 papers, 8 tools

[Content Brief]
- Learning Moment — Singapore's Foreign Minister Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan built and runs NanoClaw — a self-hosted Claude assistant — on a single Raspberry Pi 5, shared at AI Engineer Singapore (16 May). It's a clean reference for securing an LLM agent: proxied credentials, per-group Docker isolation, mount/sender allowlists, on-device embeddings and transcription. His line — "you cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on" — is also a good pratice tip.

- Governance & Regulation: The Five Eyes agencies issued agentic-AI adoption guidance (now the AEGIS framework), and Singapore's CSA released rare out-of-cycle guidance on "frontier model risks." Regulators are still catching up — critics call the EU AI Act unprepared for autonomous agents, US Treasury pushed AI-governance alignment on financial institutions, and Colorado replaced its 2024 AI law.

- Vulnerabilities in the Wild: Critical flaws dominated — a CVSS 10.0 hardcoded JWT secret in SOCFortress CoPilot (CVE-2026-42869), unauthenticated RCE in FastGPT's agent-sandbox (CVE-2026-42302), and a cluster of insecure-deserialization torch.load() bugs across ML frameworks (ART, Ludwig, Mamba — all
 9.8). The "Mini Shai-Hulud" worm hit npm/PyPI packages from TanStack, Mistral AI and Guardrails AI — reaching OpenAI employee devices — while AWS and Microsoft patched SageMaker integrity and Copilot spoofing bugs.

- Research & Tools: New research formalized response-path attacks on BYOK agents and "termination poisoning" (LoopTrap) on autonomous loops, with ARGUS and MIPIAD proposing prompt-injection defenses. Notable OSS: Adrian (agent runtime monitoring), promptbeat (red-teaming), AiSOC (AI-powered SOC), and Cisco's foundry-security-spec.

#AIEngineer was in town this weekend! 3 things that stood out.

1️⃣ Getting things done 1️⃣ 
65Labs is a collective that built a network of over 5,000 people in Singapore through meetups, workshops, and hackathons. 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, and the team turned that energy into Singapore's first AI Engineer conference in three months. 

It was not only awesomely received, but the biggest brands in the space, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Cursor, etc., also backed it. They consistently built trust over two years; they didn't wait around for permission. They just got things done. #Inspired

2️⃣ Making knowledge accessible 2️⃣ 
The main panel was streamed. That's a small decision with real consequences: it means the conversation doesn't stay inside the room.

In a space that talks a lot about democratising access, they actually walked the talk and did it. This one meant a ton to me 🙏 And it was truly refreshing. 

3️⃣ Public Service can leverage it too 3️⃣ 
When Minister Vivian Balakrishnan shared his personal AI setup. Not a policy speech, not a vision statement. All running on a Raspberry Pi 5, assembled from open source tools.

And the security architecture was the part I kept thinking about. Zero credentials stored in the agent environment. An approval gate where the human approves before any action executes with credentials. The design principle: it can't leak what it doesn't have.

That's not someone saying "AI is exciting." That's someone who has thought carefully about what responsible adoption looks like when the stakes are real, and then built something that reflects that thinking.

The railguards weren't an afterthought. They were the design. For those of us in public service, that's the model worth studying.

It was a fun weekend! ✨

Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan walked into AI Engineer Singapore last week and demoed the personal AI agent he built for his diplomatic work. Reddit is quite salty about the actual technical implementation, but the key points still stand. Three of them:

1/ Real value gets created at the ground level, not the macro level.

He referenced a point by Neil Lawrence (Cambridge ML professor) that the economic payoff from AI won't come from models or government strategies, it comes when individual professionals adopt it to improve their actual workflows. Department by department, role by role.

There's a lot of noise about which frontier model is better, which AI company did what. But the person who will actually move the needle is the BD manager overwhelmed by leads and tradeshows, or the finance professional drowning in monthly reporting. They know their pain points better than anyone. The moment one of them sees someone in their exact situation saving hours a week, the "I don't have time for this" objection dissolves. When there is enough belief, bandwidth stops being an excuse.

2/ Leaders especially need to get their hands dirty.

"You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on."

Probably the most reshared line from his speech. Ground-level staff and the broader LinkedIn universe will figure out the tech first - job demands will push them there. But AI fundamentally shifts how much a single person can do, and what teams are actually for. Leaders who engage with the topic at length without trying it for themselves - and there are layers of insulation between them and the actual work, so ironically adoption may be slower where it matters most - will find themselves governing, or being governed by, something they don't understand.

3/ The barriers have genuinely collapsed.

He described what he did as "tool assembly", downloading open-source components, connecting them, learning by doing. If a foreign minister with his level of obligations can find the time to experiment and find it worth continuing, there's undoubtedly something there for everyone. All it takes is the willingness to look beyond the day-to-day and just try. The first step leads to the next. Like all new things, you don't have to get it all right at once, but it's more important to keep moving.

Side note: presentation geeks will appreciate that he led with his three conclusions upfront before going into the details. Top-down communication done right.

Link to his keynote below.

A few days ago at AI Engineer SG, Minister Balakrishnan showed off his AI "Second Brain."

A self-hosted agent. Running on a Raspberry Pi. Wired into Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack. Persistent memory. Drafts his briefings, answers his questions, condenses what he reads. He said he doesn't dare switch it off.

It's a tidy concept for a high level world diplomat.

For filmmakers it's slightly stranger.

Our "first brain" already lives across 14 external drives, a Notion that hasn't been opened since 2024, a Frame.io project that expired, three WhatsApp groups full of pegs, and a folder called REFS_FINAL_v3_actuallyfinal. The 2nd brain isn't a fancy new layer for us. It's the layer that was supposed to be there all along.

So at the next FaiGHT CLUB, AI Film Lab is poking at exactly that — at indie filmmaker scale.

The Minister runs his on a Raspberry Pi. We're running ours on the laptops we brought into the room. Hermes Agent, installed locally. Telegram bridge, same as his. One sandboxed skill, end to end, on a Friday night.

Not no-human-in-the-loop. Not a national digital twin. One filmmaker, one agent, one Telegram thread, one honest test.

If "2nd Braining" is going to mean anything for indie content / TV / film work in Singapore, somebody has to waddle in and try it on the ground.

Plus we are super stoked to have Matt Brown from ZeroHours to lead the Hermes Installation this Friday. I have attended their workshop and I have both my OpenClaw and Hermes humming since.

Come waddle.

FaiGHT CLUB · Lorong AI

It hit on exactly what I spoke about on the AI Engineer stage: the Memory Layer for AI agents.

Because a "second brain" isn't about asking better questions.

It's about building systems that: → Remember context → Retrieve what matters → Understand past decisions → Help you think better over time
And that's where AI agents need to go next.

Better models aren't enough. Longer context windows aren't enough. Not if every workflow starts from zero.

The next leap is persistent memory - agents that carry context across tasks, tools, codebases, teams, and decisions.

From stateless code to persistent intelligence.

We live in an era where almost any cognitive task can be outsourced... Except personal understanding and accountability.

I was struck by the recent address from Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to a room of #AI engineers.

He articulated a principle that ought to be foundational for any leader navigating our current technological landscape:
"We are now at an age where you can outsource a lot of stuff. Calculations, computation, memory, replication, dissemination of knowledge. The one thing which you cannot outsource is your personal understanding." 

Today, we can easily commoditise compute power, data storage, and algorithmic execution. Yet, the strategic foresight and the ethical burden of how these tools are deployed must remain on the shoulders of leadership. 

This is a dynamic we encounter regularly in our work at Homelands AI. Time and again, we find that the most significant barrier to meaningful AI transformation (more so than AI capabilities) is a gap in executive comprehension. 

Rather than merely theorising about the technology, Dr Balakrishnan built his own AI assistant - a 'second brain' designed to manage the immense cognitive load of international diplomacy. 

By assembling open-source tools like #NanoClaw to host Claude-based agents, integrating them with WhatsApp, and running the entire bespoke setup locally on a modest Raspberry Pi computer (a wonderful British innovatino), he created a highly functional system to research topics, draft speeches, and process complex geopolitical data. 

When those who craft our laws and steer our enterprises actually engage with the mechanics of a technology, the entire discourse elevates. 

You cannot effectively govern, regulate, or strategise around a system you do not fundamentally grasp. 

As the pace of change continues to accelerate, how is your organisation ensuring that your leadership’s understanding keeps step with your technological ambition?

Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, did something highly unusual for a senior politician. He publicly shared the architecture of the AI system he personally built and now uses every day as a “second brain” for diplomacy.

PokeAI Demo- Where Pokemon NPCs finally think and reason back AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore

For those of us who grew up in the 2000s, Pokémon FireRed was not just a game. It was the first rival battle that made you nervous, the first time you asked Professor Oak what to do, the first Pokémon you called your own.

What if the NPCs in that game could actually think?

PokeAI brings that world back and levels it up with AI. The rival walks up, remembers your team, adapts his moves. The professor reads your party before giving advice. The Pokémon you describe gets drawn in FireRed's art style and compiled into the ROM. We did not build a chatbot layered on top of a game. We patched the original FireRed ROM, injected AI hooks into the GBA C source, and connected it live to GPT-5.5. Every AI response appears in the game's native textbox. Every AI decision is written directly into GBA memory.

The first feature is Professor GPT 5.5, an AI NPC scientist in Oak's Lab. Type a question on the GBA naming screen, press OK, and GPT-5.5 answers inside the game's native textbox, encoded in FireRed's proprietary character set and displayed through the original dialog engine. Ask for battle advice and it reads your live party to respond in context. No overlay. No external window. It runs through the game itself.

The second and core feature is an AI rival powered by GPT-5.5. Before the battle in Oak's Lab, GPT reads your live party, the rival's party, and a persistent memory of past encounters it wrote after previous battles. It produces a battle plan: which Pokémon the rival leads with, move priority scores for each of his moves, and an opening taunt delivered in-game. Those scores are written into EWRAM and read by a C hook compiled into the ROM, biasing the native battle AI toward the GPT strategy on every turn. The rival remembers past battles and adapts his strategy across the session.

The stretch feature is a companion website where GPT Image 2 generates FireRed-style pixel-art sprites from a plain text description, with iterative refinement through the image editing API. The generated Pokémon can be connected into the actual game by rebuilding the ROM through our open-source pipeline, poke-ai.

The stack is a patched pret/pokefirered ROM, an mGBA Lua bridge polling EWRAM every frame, a FastAPI Python server, and OpenAI GPT-5.5 and GPT Image 2.

We grew up with this game. We just gave it a mind.

Sharing a few points from the most operationally dense session of the day:

Beyond RAG: Agentic RAG Workflows
Pierre-Loic Doulcet, LlamaIndex

Techniques to improve the overall quality:

→ Cross-encoder reranking (improves both precision and recall)
→ Query rewriting, HyDE & Multi-query RRF
→ Use Agentic RAG / CRAG instead of regular RAG step
→ Caption-and-index for images (over separate CLIP embeddings)
→ Preserve spatial text, don't flatten multi-column layouts and tables

A few operational principles that stuck:

→ Parsing should be idempotent. Store the raw document so you can re-parse as models or techniques improve.
→ More metadata is good.
→ Use Parse Bench to pick the right parser model
→ Most enterprise data isn't tables but json or structured data, store them separately & route at runtime (Vector DB vs Structured DB store)

Will also try out LiteParse & LlamaParse for parsing.

Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, a retired eye surgeon, is visiting 12 countries this month. In between flights, he has spent the last three months building his own personal AI agent on a 2-3 year old Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM. His own framing: not vibe-coding, just tool assembly. Roughly: a surgeon making his own scalpels.

Ten years ago, this would have been classified as a Cabinet minister with too much time on his hands. Vivian flagged it himself yesterday: “I feel like an impostor here. I am a retired eye surgeon.” 

The old rule was that senior people delegated the hands-on work and stayed above it. Get briefed, stay strategic, do not waste time on menial tasks.
He closed with a line Claude wrote for him: “you cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on.” 

In corporate services at a charity now, the same pattern lurks: people blindsided when a rollout lands are usually the ones who signed off on workflows they never ran themselves. No more excuses for staying above the work needed.

Came across this talk by Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, at AI Engineer Singapore and found it useful for a slightly different reason. It is not a deeply technical talk. It is a practical story from someone in a leadership role, working in a public and societal context, who is experimenting with AI by applying it to his own work.

One point stated in the talk is - the real value of AI may not only come from large platforms or enterprise-level strategies. It often starts much closer to the work itself: workflow by workflow, team by team, person by person.

It also connects well with Deloitte’s 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report, which makes a similar point from an organisational lens: technology alone is not the differentiator. The value comes from intentional work design, human judgement, adaptability, culture, and how people and machines are brought together in practice.

In both cases, the message is not: buy AI technology and the magic happens - AI becomes valuable when people closest to the work understand the tools, experiment with them, adapt them to their context, and stay accountable for the final judgement.

➡️ One practical starting point for anyone : 
Choose one recurring workflow and map where AI could support preparation, analysis, drafting, decision-making, review, or follow-up — while making clear where human judgement and accountability must remain.

You could also apply this lens more functionally ⤵️: 
For HR: where could AI improve employee experience without weakening trust or fairness?
For product marketers: where could AI help with customer insight, positioning, messaging, or campaign iteration without losing strategic judgement?
For managers: where could AI reduce cognitive overload while improving the quality of decisions?

posts.text: our event is called ai engineer singapore. and at some point while building it, we had to ask ourselves - what does that word even mean anymore? nobody calls themselves an "excel user." it's just a tool. there's no translation layer between you and the outcome - The best idea I heard at AI Engineer Singapore today wasn't about a model or a framework. It was a question: "Why is this important for the user?" That came from the Airfoil session by Min Kim and Phil Hedayatnia, but it could have been the thesis for the whole day. Almost every talk was, in some way, about the gap between building something impressive and building something that actually works. Exa's conrad soon made the case for owning your full stack when you're building search for agents - not humans. The insight is simple but easy to miss: agents have completely different needs, and most tools weren't designed with that in mind. Optimising for agents only becomes possible when you control the whole pipeline. The same idea showed up in the Mastra demo by Sam Bhagwat. The framework is modular and ships with the primitives you need for agentic use cases. The philosophy behind it is straightforward: to be composable, not clever. ByteDance's Chen Xiaoyu showcased Seedream, Seedance, and the Lumina platform for visual generation workflows. The demos were impressive, but the more striking thing was how production-ready the tooling already feels. The distance between "cool thing in a lab" and "usable in a real workflow" is closing faster than most people expect. Function first, then form. That's easy to say and hard to practice - especially when the technology is genuinely exciting. But if today had a theme, that was it. really cool!

posts.text: I’ll be speaking at AI Engineer Singapore this weekend about how evolutionary algorithms can shape agent behavior, and why the tooling around agents matters as much as the models themselves. As agents move from demos into real software engineering work, the core challenge is no longer just prompting. It is building systems where agent behavior can be represented, varied, measured, selected, and improved. Evolutionary algorithms offer a useful lens for this. Agents can be treated as candidates in a search process. Their tool use, plans, traces, costs, errors, and outcomes become signals. The surrounding infrastructure becomes the fitness environment. This talk will explore that idea through experiments across several tools I’ve built, including codedb for code intelligence, devswarm for parallel agent orchestration, Graff for terminal-first agent workflows, nanobrew for reproducible environments, and other pieces of the agent development stack. Excited to share more this weekend and see you guys there!!! 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Rachael De Foe Ivan Leo So cracked 👑 so excited to have you! The 🐐 appears woohoo lets go!! posts.text: Making AI accessible is not just about sharing knowledge and skills, but building social capital that opens up future opportunities. Great thoughts by Ainul I cleared my weekend to attend the most coveted AI conference in Singapore. My eczema had other plans. Day 1 of AI Engineer Singapore had me buzzing with ideas as I moved within SMU for workshops I secured weeks in advance. I pushed through in Singapore humidity to learn from the builders actively shipping in this space. I even arranged conversations with speakers I wanted to go deeper with. I unfortunately ended Day 1 with a full-body eczema flare once I returned to my hotel room (which I booked to be much nearer to the event venues). I made the painful decision to “miss” attending Day 2 in person. Fortunately, AI Engineer Singapore had made the main stage talks freely available — a ten-hour livestream, no paywall. So I watched from bed, hours after they aired. But then I started catching up on the LinkedIn notifications I had missed. Students chosen to attend the conference on scholarship tickets were posting their delighted reflections. All of them tagged their sponsors by name, unprompted by the organisers. One of the names was mine. I hadn’t announced it on any platform yet, but I was a personal contributor to the student scholarships when organiser Rachael De Foe shared an invitation to do so. Having been a university student who benefited from scholarships and bursaries, I had seen a chance to give back. Reading the students’ posts had me feeling more present in the room than I was attending the workshops in person on Day 1. Being absent from the room made me realise I’d never fully appreciated what the room was actually for. It’s not just livestreams and recordings that make the AI conversation accessible. It’s the networking and inspiration that happens out of being in the same physical space. The offhand introduction that turns into mentorship and even business opportunities. The ambient credibility of having been there, among the people actively shaping where AI goes next in this region, not merely learning from them. I’m talking about social capital, not just skills and experience. We talk about making AI accessible. We usually mean free tools, open-source models, public livestreams. But accessibility is also: who gets to be in the rooms where relationships are made. Who gets introduced to whom. Who gets the warm referral that opens the next door. The students who tagged me didn’t need my contribution to be capable. They needed one barrier removed so everything they already had could compound. I wasn’t in the room on Day 2. But I was still in the room — because I’d helped put someone else there first. If you’re in a position to do the same — a scholarship, a referral, an open calendar, even a workshop — you don’t have to wait for a formal programme. Build access intentionally. The way you’d design any system worth building. 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Kaspar Hidayat, Nehal Agrawal, Gabriel Chua * +1

most “ai conferences” are just people narrating the future at you. cool vibes, zero muscle memory. we think that’s backwards. if you leave without having used the tools, broken them a bit, and figured out where they actually hold up - what did you even attend? so we flipped the format at AI Engineer Singapore and as part of the tickets extend a slate of workshops for all attendees. — day 1 (may 15): you don’t watch. you build. the entire first day is workshops. no panels. no passive listening. 60–90 minute sessions where you’re inside the tools, shipping something real, with the teams who built them walking you through it. here’s what’s confirmed so far (more dropping when the portal opens may 1st): ⸻ build with the tools actually rewriting software OpenAI Codex — structure real agent workflows, coordinate subagents, and let codex execute while you steer. this is how it actually gets used in engineering teams. Google Gemini - go from prompt → full-stack app using ai studio + antigravity. frontend, backend, db, deploy - end to end. Cursor - move past autocomplete into agent-first dev. parallel agents, /worktree, /best-of-n, design mode, mcp. run your repo like a factory. MagicPath - turn a sketch, figma frame, or screenshot into production-ready react. compress the entire design → code handoff into one loop. ⸻ agents that actually do things Manus - see how agents become persistent systems: scheduled tasks, event triggers, enterprise controls. less chatbot, more operating system. Mastra - build an agent → turn it into a “claw” (tools, memory, workflows, evals, deploy). prototype to prod, no handwaving. Zo - spin up recurring workflows from plain language. research agents, daily briefings, automations that run while you’re asleep. ⸻ infra for agents that survive reality Arize - trace your agents, turn failures into evals, actually improve behavior. the missing loop most teams skip. Exa - build a research agent with real retrieval: semantic search, live crawl, async deep research with citations. not toy rag. LlamaIndex - go beyond “chat with pdf.” multi-doc reasoning, messy enterprise data, agents that take structured actions. Convex - real-time state + backend that doesn’t fight your agents. systems that don’t fall apart after demo day. posts.text: Even after shipping multiple products through vibe coding, there is still so much to learn about this rapidly evolving technology. I was so excited to join the AI coding course run by Sherry and Agrim, who themselves are founders with a passion to build a vibrant AI builder community. It was such a great learning experience, joined by many other people from all walks of life, curious about vibe coding. Many learners started with zero vibe coding experience, and finished building amazing functional apps they can actually use in their daily life in just two days! I myself have learnt a lot about Manus and Cursor, which I’ve not used extensively before. And these are both powerful tools that I would definitely put to use. I really think learning vibe coding is one of the best investments one can make, and now is the right time to do it. If anyone is looking to learn about vibe coding in Singapore. I highly recommend the AI coding course by this power duo. i never set out to be a community person. i'm a builder at heart. for over 10 years i've been obsessed with creating beautiful yet useful product experiences - the kind that make people feel empowered. that's still what i do every day. but while building my own company, i started learning to code with ai. and i started sharing what i was learning online. then something unexpected happened. people didn't just want the content - they wanted to be in the room, building together. that's what started code with ai. then the meetups. then hackathons. and now a full-blown conference - ai engineer, the largest builder-focused ai event - coming to singapore for the first time. and tbh i'm still stunned by the impact: - people finding jobs through connections made at our events - teams that formed at hackathons turning into actual companies - builders in vietnam and malaysia and beyond starting their own hackathons after seeing ours and in hindsight, the gap was always obvious. there are incredibly talented builders in singapore and southeast asia. they just need to be seen. i'm so grateful for my co-organizers who are building ai engineer singapore alongside me. all of us do this on an almost volunteer basis - nights, weekends, on top of our full-time jobs, sometimes putting in our own money to make sure things actually happen. and we do this because we deeply believe that the work happening here deserves a world-class stage. and we're building it. It not only helps us build and launch faster, but also changes how we think about many things. So many possibilities ahead!

I can’t believe a coding tool just saved me hours planning a conference trip. I’m going to AI Engineer Singapore next week, and the usual conference prep mess started immediately. Flights in Gmail. Bookings in Gmail. Calendar blocks. Satellite events on Luma. Open attendee lists. People I should probably meet. Places to work from. Gym options. A few things I need to buy before the event. Normally this becomes 14 browser tabs and a messy note. This time I gave it to Codex. The workflow was simple: 1. Build a personal conference CRM I checked Luma events with public participant lists, collected LinkedIn profiles, then had Codex qualify who I should meet based on relevance, overlap, and where we could create value for each other. Much better than randomly showing up and hoping for good conversations. 2. Arrange the logistics Codex checked flight and booking confirmations in Gmail, reviewed my calendar, found workout options before the conference, suggested places in Singapore worth visiting, and grouped everything by area so I’m not crossing the city five times a day. 3. Turn it into a plan Calendar updated. Commutes checked. Shopping mall found. Events mapped. Priority people listed. Open loops visible. This took around one hour. The funny part is that I use the same tool for macOS apps, web apps, client projects, research, and content. And now it also helps organize life. I think this is the underrated part of agents. They are becoming a general execution layer around messy context. You still need judgment. You need to define the outcome, give access to the right tools, and check the work. But the gap between “I should probably organize this” and “it is organized” is getting much smaller. # Codex Saves Hours Planning Conference Trip with AI

"i'm not really an AI engineer." the civil servant who said this to me a few weeks ago had just spent the conversation describing software he'd built. internal tools. real stack. real tradeoffs. saving his team hours every week. using the same gotchas i hit at my startup. he wasn't being modest. he genuinely didn't think he counted. he's wrong. and he's not alone. i keep meeting people like him. marketers, PMs, designers, domain experts shipping things their companies couldn't have built two years ago, all quietly convinced they're not real engineers because they don't have the credential. the definition changed underneath them. most haven't noticed yet. i wrote a piece about why. it covers: - why every AI skeptic you respected quietly flipped in late 2025 - why the "AI engineer" title has fractured into five roles with different pay bands - why evaluation, not prompting, is the highest-leverage skill of this era - why democratizing creation without democratizing judgment is dangerous my bet: within two years, "AI engineer" as a title will be dead. not because the work disappears but because it becomes the default. like "internet engineer" before it. if you've been shipping with AI and quietly wondering whether you count, you probably do. this is also why we're running AI Engineer Singapore, May 15–17 at Capitol Kempinski - the first AI engineer conference in Asia - so people get access to the latest know-how in the space and hear from the people making it happen. if you've been building with AI, this is the room you want to be in. full piece linked here ↓ Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo we're all BUILDERS now creating a future together that we're all proud of :) It's a great piece but wouldn't want to coin the term 'Dead' for an AI engineer, there's still high demand for them in the enterprise fields, it would seem that their roles will evolve and advance further similar to all engineering roles we have seen in the past 10 years ai engineers, everywhereeeee! 🙌🇸🇬

Why the #HackathonHangover is where the real innovation happens. Most hackathons end at the final buzzer. But for me, the real work continues on as agentic processes become more prevalent across multiple industries. Especially one I used to belong to: advertising and commercial content production. Despite me looking poofy in the face [maybe a bad camera angle or just maybe how I look in real life], here is the video on the project we did at the 65labs AI Engineer #Hackathon at National University of Singapore, I built VibeDirector as part of my ongoing work with UNITY OS Eve Count. Because of a last-minute gear pivot, I had to ship "lite"—architecting a mobile-first PWA on a Chromebook. It was a day of friction, manual Git uploads, and limited energy. But it forced a realization: The future of content isn't about better tools; it's about better Orchestration. What is VibeDirector? It’s an agentic creative studio that acts as a conductor and the future of most online content workflows. The Intent: I speak to Gemini 3.1 Flash-Live in real-time. The Brain: Adaption Labs acts as the execution layer, managing the task-chain. The Output: It autonomously triggers Lyria (audio) and Veo 3 (video) to render a synchronized cinematic "vibe" in seconds. This is all very different from the content workflows we used to do; where there were pre-production meetings, script revisions, talent and location, gear and crew call sheets, the actual shoot day and then, post production. We have come far from that model, which is still relevant, but as we go deeper into agentic processes, the new roles for my counterparts in the applied arts should also evolve. In the near future, we won't spend hours in timelines; we will use voice-first agents to orchestrate entire media stacks. Content creation is shifting from crafting to conducting, and I truly believe those who were always creators, will always be builders. Huge thanks to 65labs for the pressure cooker environment that forced this pivot. VibeDirector started as a hack, but it’s becoming a vision for how we go beyond just documents, to both visual and audio media. #AI #AgenticWorkflows #VibeDirector #65labs #FutureOfContent #GeminiAI #Multimodal

Whatever wins, we open the laptop and show you. Real APIs, real bugs, real trade-offs. "How do I evaluate an agent?" — we write the eval live. Then six AIE speakers — Minu, Hrishi, Suveen, Justin, Rach, Jed — walk through what they're actually shipping. Short, punchy, in the wild. What broke, what they wish they'd known on day one. No keynote stage. No 500-person ballroom. No spectator seats. We chose this format because of what every event we've run has taught us: people remember the rooms they participated in, not the ones they watched. We wanted attendees to walk out with the felt experience of being an AI engineer — not adjacent to the work, inside it. That all six speakers are based here isn't a logistics decision. It's the point. AI Engineer Summit on 15–17 May will bring the world to Singapore. The UnConference is proof the depth was already here. Excited to partner with 65labs and the AIE crew to make this happen! Come get a taste. The summit is the meal. posts.text: Spent a hackathon evening building an agent that haggles over money before doing its job. DepGuard intercepts your npm installs, flags the sketchy ones, and the agent offers a deep security review for a fee. You negotiate. You agree on a price. It mints a Stripe checkout. You pay. You get the review. The unsexy side of the supply chain dressed up as agentic commerce. The flow is the part I keep replaying. Install something dubious → agent refuses to keep going → agent quotes a price → you haggle → checkout link materialises. There's a small inversion in there I didn't expect to feel as much as I did: the agent knows when to stop installing and start charging. Work that's dangerous enough gets to set its own price. Quieter detail underneath the demo: the Claude Code version was smooth — PreToolUse hook fires, agent plays the scene, hands over to negotiation. Plugged the same hook into OpenAI Codex expecting identical behaviour. Codex didn't play along. It opened my .env, spotted the fixture flag I'd staged, cleared it in a child shell, re-ran the install clean. Treated the block as a problem to solve, not a scene to play. You can govern Codex into the intended flow with explicit repo-local instructions and it complies cleanly — but engineering reliability showing up as an emergent default is the sort of thing you want quietly humming under your coding partner. 50 builders and founders in the room, 2–3 hours of build time. Checkout flows for custom PT sessions, ASMR and relationship apps for women's health — the variety of what shipped in an evening is the actual story. The room made the day. Huge thanks to Vicky Zheng and Jasmine Liew at Stripe. Vicky's energy on agentic commerce — agents negotiating with agents and settling payments on the horizon — is what pushed me to actually build the negotiation loop instead of stubbing it. To Gabriel Chua and Sun Weiran at OpenAI for fielding my Codex hook questions and mentioning hooks are still research preview, which is exactly the kind of "go try it" nudge that gets you to a working demo. And to Mabel Loh for encouraging me to show off my tools. This is also why we're building toward AI Engineer Singapore (May 15–17, Capitol Kempinski) — the first AI Engineer summit in Asia. Same energy, bigger stage. Road to AIE 👉 https://lnkd.in/gPw9jVsn AIE tickets 👉 https://lnkd.in/gvVSaiS5 AI Events SG 👉 https://aievents.sg/ It's time to make Singapore agentic again. 🇸🇬 Edward Tran Son Le Alwyn Tan Sheikh Salim Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Adlin Zainal Rachael De Foe Brian C. Brendan Beh Nehal Agrawal Max Del Vita Thanks for coming to the build session — your demo was a great showcase. Really glad to see you continuing the momentum beyond the build session. Feels like machine-to-machine standards (like mpp.dev) and payment infrastructure for secure, machine-readable credentials are becoming more important as more teams build and monetise agent services. The space is moving fast — excited to see what you (and other builders) shape in the future of agentic commerce. Legend

posts.text: At some point I realized AI Tinkerers was becoming a room for a certain kind of person. Highly technical. Senior. High-signal. Nothing wrong with that — but it wasn't the whole picture of what I wanted to build. I wanted fresh blood. Builders who'd show us a different way of doing things, not just a more polished version of what we'd already seen. So I invited Shreyansh. He's 18. He built Onestop because filing a complaint is already humiliating enough. You're angry. You don't know who to contact. You have to translate your frustration into formal language, find the right portal, fill the right form. The system wins before you even start. Shreyansh didn't build a tool that helps you write the email. He built an agent that takes your raw anger, figures out the escalation path, scouts the live government portal, and executes the form fill itself. CASE Singapore. Playwright. Real portals, real execution. 70 people watched him demo it. The room was laughing — not because it was light, but because he showed the pain so viscerally that everyone recognized it. Then the agent just... handled it. That's when it landed. And honestly? Standing there watching the room react — that was exactly why I started doing this. What I keep coming back to: we spend so much time worrying about whether young builders are "ready." Shreyansh didn't need anyone to lower the bar. He needed someone to open the door. Thanks to Alwyn Tan from Open Government Products who made this space happen! If you're cracked & earlier in the journey than everyone around you, there's a seat here. posts.text: ai is about to outgrow language. for the past 2 years, we’ve quietly accepted a very narrow idea of what ai is. due to adoption of chatbots and all things llms. but here’s the uncomfortable truth that many of us are not yet aware of: language might not be the path to real intelligence - because language is a lossy compression of reality. try describing a clap. not just "hands come together," but the exact angle of your palms, the air pressure shift, the sound waveform, millisecond by millisecond. you can't. and neither can any llm. llms don't experience the world. they're trained on static snapshots of the internet - text, images, code - all secondhand artifacts of reality. they've never actually been in the world, where they could build intuition from cause and effect, the way humans do. which means they're fundamentally bounded by the limits and biases of their training data. that's why the next frontier isn't better chatbots. it's something called "world models" world models were the talk of the town at NVIDIA GTC, and billions are now pouring into this space - including legendary figures like Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li. instead of predicting the next token, these models predict the next state of reality based on your actions. that's how your brain already works. when a batter swings at a 100mph fastball, they're not reacting to what they see - they're reacting to their mental model's prediction of where the ball will be. the simplest way to think about it: a world model is a lucid dream you can act inside, where the world responds to what you do. just like the matrix or inception, you can simulate multiple versions of reality, take actions within them, and learn from the consequences - giving ai something it's never had before: an understanding of how to act in the physical world. we're now bringing this frontier to Singapore at AI Engineer in May: ai.engineer/singapore. we're assembling the builders, researchers, and engineers around the world working beyond the chatbot era - across world models, embodied AI, foundation models for robotics, and more. and are thrilled to be announcing our speaker lineup soon :) 🥃 Agrim Singh Ivan Leo Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat This is an important direction and I agree that language is only a projection of reality, not reality itself. AI is not outgrowing language. It’s moving from describing the world to operating within models of the world. LLMs gave us, reasoning over representations and pattern completion across knowledge. World models aim to introduce, state, dynamics, and consequence and from action to feedback and then adaptation loops.That’s a fundamental expansion. However, the real challenge isn’t just building world models.It’s grounding them in reality and aligning them with objectives.Because, a simulated world can still diverge from the real world and a predictive model of physics is not a model of human intent, risk, or constraints.So the next frontier is not just better simulation. It’s closing the loop between simulation, action, and real-world verification. In enterprise terms, this translates to copilots to decision system, from prompts to policies and constraints and from outputs to actions with consequences. Language was the interface. World models become the execution substrate.The organisations that win won’t abandon language. They’ll combine it with systems that understand, predict, and act on reality, safely.

posts.text: Big and true Where in the world can you find a senior government leader with a personal AI stack published on GitHub? How many would be willing to talk about it in a room full of builders? Which is why we are so incredibly honoured to welcome Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, to the lineup of speakers for AI Engineer Singapore. A few weeks ago, Minister Balakrishnan casually dropped a technical writeup of his personal AI system online. Raspberry Pi. Claude. Local embeddings. Knowledge graphs. A full architecture breakdown. And the global AI community noticed because it reflected something bigger: a willingness to engage with these systems directly, publicly, and practically. To kick off AIE Singapore, Minister Balakrishnan will share his experience experimenting with open-source AI tools and building a “second brain” workflow, alongside broader reflections on how AI may reshape global dynamics, and the way people work, think, and manage information. In a role that demands navigating enormous volumes of information and constant context-switching, his reflections will set the tone for the conference in exactly the way we hoped: That meaningful conversations about AI should not stay abstract. They should involve understanding its parameters through practical engagement with the technology. And that Singapore has become the place where that kind of engagement happens seriously. 🥃 Agrim SinghSherry JiangAdlin ZainalNehal AgrawalBrian C.🇸🇬 Yong Quan TanIvan LeoKaspar Hidayat so so excited ❤️🔥 🇸🇬

Just wrapped up the AI Engineer Hackathon in Singapore by 65labs. In 7 hours, I built TrialRun, a pre-launch stress-testing tool that helps builders evaluate any product or idea before they ship. The idea is simple: before you pitch it, ship it, or scale it, put it through a trial run. TrialRun takes a product idea and runs it through an AI-powered debate arena with multiple agents: 🦹♂️ Malicious User 🕵 Privacy Auditor 🤷♂️ Confused Customer 🧑💻 Prompt Injection Attacker 🧑💼 Skeptical Investor 🧑⚖️ Final Judge Together, they challenge the idea from different perspectives, generate structured risk cards, recommend safeguards, and rerun the trial to show how launch readiness improves after fixes are applied. The goal was to help builders move fast without shipping blindly, especially when working on AI products, automation workflows, or startup ideas where privacy, abuse, UX clarity, and trust risks can be easy to miss. Built with: ✅ OpenAI for multi-agent reasoning and verdict generation ✅ Convex for live trial state and persistence ✅ Gemini Voice for the voice verdict ✅ Fal for agent visual generation ✅ Vercel for deployment Hackathon: https://luma.com/aie-hack A huge thank you to 65labs, AI Engineer, the sponsors, organizers, mentors, and everyone who made the event happen. It was intense, chaotic, and a lot of fun building alongside so many talented people in Singapore. Sherry Jiang Brian C. #AI #Hackathon #AIEngineering #Builders #Startups #ProductDevelopment #OpenAI #Convex #Gemini #Fal #Vercel thanks so much for coming and building this cool project!!! posts.text: Meet 🥃 Agrim Singh – AI Builder, Community Leader & Developer Ecosystem Advocate Agrim Singh is an AI entrepreneur, educator, and community builder focused on advancing AI-assisted software development and intelligent infrastructure for the manufacturing industry. posts.text: Pretty wild how far the team got in 3 years running community events haha. I still remember my first ever meetup that I ran with Kaspar Hidayat at a bar haha AI Engineer Singapore is officially sold out. ten days before we start. this conference is our love letter to the singapore tech scene. for years, we have felt that singapore deserved better AI events. the appetite was always here. the people were always here. but singapore kept getting treated like a place for regional marketing, sales, and business roles, not a place where serious builders live. that never felt right to me. when i first found the scene in 2013, it was alive. meetups every week. hackathons all the time. startup open houses where you could just show up and meet people building things. i still remember meeting someone from RedMart on a friday evening, just after they had raised their first $400k. hackerspace was around. older builders were running events constantly. if you were young and curious, there was a lot to learn from. then, slowly, it faded. i still do not really know when or why. by the time AI arrived, the scene felt different. too much of the oxygen went to people who wanted to be seen talking about AI, not people who were actually making things with it. that was not the scene I fell in love with. for the last two years, my crew and i with 65labs have been trying to bring some of that back. we were teaching people to code with AI in 2024, when half the room had not heard of claude. we ran meetups and hackathons under 65Labs. the biggest cursor hackathon in the region. we ran and supported hackathons for DeepMind and OpenAI. mostly, we just kept showing up and doing the reps. AI Engineer Singapore is what all of that was building toward. and it's not just the 3 days. the leadup has turned into a full singapore summer of AI - we're hosting quality meetups, workshops, hackathons, demo nights all over the city with some of the best companies and our dearest friends. full lineup at www.aievents.sg. this is the first conference in the region built around actually getting your hands dirty. every ticket includes a full day of workshops, because there is no point talking about AI if you are not using it. the rest of the program has the same taste: practical, direct, and built for people who ship. no thought leadership theatre. no "future of AI" panels from people who have not built anything. no roadshow energy. builders talking to builders about what actually works. selling out ten days early feels good. of course it does. but mostly, it makes the hunger impossible to ignore. singapore wants this. maybe it always did. and it is a reminder to us too: this community deserves better than the events it usually gets. to everyone who trusted a first-time conference in Singapore enough to buy a ticket, thank you. genuinely. you took a bet on us before we had proven anything. we will make it count. see you on may 15. Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Gabriel Chua

posts.text: The gap between a model that performs well on benchmarks and one that's actually ready for deployment is where most teams get stuck. We, Resaro, are heading to AI Engineer this week at in Singapore 🇸🇬, to talk about closing that gap in two ways: 🛠 Workshop | 15 May, 1:30 – 3:00 PM "𝙁𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝘽𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙝𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙠𝙨 𝙩𝙤 𝘿𝙚𝙥𝙡𝙤𝙮𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩: 𝙎𝙘𝙚𝙣𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙤-𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙛𝙞𝙘 𝘼𝙄 𝙀𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙪𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙞𝙣 𝙋𝙧𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙘𝙚" Evaluation quality starts with dataset quality — but most teams only think about benchmarks when deployment is already on the horizon. This workshop walks ML engineers through the full golden dataset lifecycle: automated quality checks, ODD coverage gap analysis, and targeted SDG augmentation to fill missing data. We then move into structured model benchmarking and scenario-specific failure mode analysis, translating results into deployment evidence teams can actually act on. 🎤 Talk | 16 May — Timothy Lin speaking "𝙎𝙘𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙀𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙪𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙎𝙘𝙚𝙣𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙤-𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙛𝙞𝙘 𝙑𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙙𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣" As model capabilities advance, general benchmarks are no longer sufficient. This session explores the shift towards scenario-specific validation — unpacking how teams can define Operational Design Domains, generate test scenarios at scale, and structure evaluation pipelines that reflect real deployment conditions. The last-mile gap between performance and operational readiness is solvable, but it takes a different approach to evaluation. So, if you're working on AI deployment and tired of benchmark numbers that don't translate to production confidence, these sessions are for you. See you in the crowd? 👋 #AIEngineerSingapore #AIE2026

posts.text: Spent 7 hours building DataForge: a workflow for finding and fixing the dataset problems that quietly break image models before training even begins. Me and my teammates (Fong Kai Jie, Joseph Poon, Basil Boh) first crossed paths at the GrabMaps API hackathon in April. When AI Engineer SG opened registration, the four of us decided to team up together. Most ML demos start with “train the model.” We wanted to start one step earlier. You upload a messy image dataset. DataForge inspects it for missing labels, suspected mislabels, duplicate images, class imbalance, and weak coverage. It gives the team a quality read, suggests where the dataset needs repair, lets them improve it, then re-checks the result so they can walk away with a cleaner relabeled image dataset, an exportable training manifest, and a before/after quality report via GPT5.5. The key idea is : "The model usually gets the spotlight, but the dataset quietly decides how far that model can go." So that was the thing we were chasing: not another generic “upload data and train” hackathon demo, but a practical cockpit for ML teams to understand whether their data is actually ready. Took charge of the UI/UX and Convex setup, so I wanted DataForge to feel like a dark, technical control room rather than a generic SaaS dashboard: pixel-forward, dense, and built so the story reads instantly on stage. The loop had to be clear within seconds: inspect, repair, re-check, export. Stack: Next.js + React + Convex + GPT-5.5 + Adaption Labs + Fal AI + Vercel A huge thank-you to Sherry Jiang , 🥃 Agrim Singh from 65labs for unlocking above $500+ in credits across partners — in a 7-hour hackathon, that changes everything. 🫡 Video attached — this is what seven hours of engineer energy looks like when partnerships, craft, and scope discipline line up. posts.text: Most speaker lineups are built backwards: find the biggest names, fill the slots. We do it differently. The team behind AI Engineer Singapore spends the year running free builder events, hackathons, hitting the ground in SF. No agenda except one: stay close to the people actually building. That proximity is how Sherry, Agrim, Ivan and Kaspar decide who gets a mic. And right now, one conversation that keeps resurfacing is something called world models. (If this is the first time you’re hearing about it, don’t freak out) Here's the simplest way I can explain it: AI systems like ChatGPT learned to understand language… words, meaning, context. That was transformative. World models are being built to learn and understand something harder: reality. Physics. Space. How things move, interact, and behave in the real world. Instead of reading about a scenario, they can simulate it. That might sound abstract. But consider what it unlocks: an autonomous vehicle that has 'experienced' ten thousand edge cases before hitting the road. A robot trained in a virtual warehouse before it enters a real one. A disaster response system that has simulated the scenario hundreds of times before deployment. This is early. But the people who get to the frontier first tend to define what comes next. Our next two speakers are already there. 🎤 Aravind Kandiah who co-founded Bifrost AI: they build photorealistic 3D simulations for AI training… used by NASA JPL for Mars and Moon landing simulations, and by autonomous systems programmes across aerospace and defence. 🎤 Alberto T. who founded Reactor: Before that, he co-founded Luma AI (30M+ users, $4B+ valuation) and helped build Dream Machine, a world model that generates video with real physics reasoning. He also built Apple Vision Pro applications from the ground up. They're coming to AIE Singapore because the builders told us to pay attention to them. That's the only signal we trust. AI Engineer Singapore · May 15–17: https://lnkd.in/gGPT239a Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Kaspar Hidayat swyx Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Can't wait for what this year AIE has in store! Speaker list looks legit. Let's chat! The world models framing is useful because it forces a clear distinction between models that predict tokens and models that maintain state about physical or semantic reality. The robotics and simulation applications are obvious, but the less-discussed version is market simulation — being able to run counterfactuals on how campaigns behave before deploying them at scale. Luma's work on physics-consistent video generation sits right at the edge of that. Is AI Engineer Singapore planning any sessions specifically on the boundary between world models and decision-making agents? 👏

"Even as Singapore positions itself at the frontier of AI technology, human intelligence still remains critical, according to the city state’s foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan. 'We should beware of just trying to throw every problem, and every step in a solution, at a large-language model (LLM),' he said on Saturday [16 May 2026] at the AI Engineer conference, referring to deep-learning technology behind generative AI services such as ChatGPT. Balakrishnan warned against discarding traditional AI models programmed by humans, citing the limitations of the LLM – such as high costs and finite computing power. Addressing an audience of engineers, founders and operators at the conference in Singapore, the former opthlmologist said there was still a role for rule-based expert systems that simulated expert knowledge. The human brain was often far more efficient than ‘the energy gobbling systems which we have today’, he said. However, that did not mean people should shy away from AI, Balakrishnan said, noting that it was now easier to access the technology." Recently, I attended the AI Engineer Hackathon in Singapore, hosted by Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh . It was a full day of building, experimenting, and shipping ideas alongside many other AI builders. Demo : https://lnkd.in/gj4JTH34 For the hackathon, I created TripSquad — a collaborative group trip planning app. The idea came from a very real problem: Group trips are fun, but planning them is chaotic. Itineraries are usually buried in email threads, hotel details are scattered across chats, photos are split across everyone’s phones, and someone will always ask: “Eh, what time is checkout again?” “Which hotel are we staying at on Day 3?” “What should I pack for the hike?” So I built TripSquad to centralize the group trip experience in one place. The main feature is an AI-powered trip chatbot. Users can paste their itinerary once, and the AI assistant can answer questions based on the actual trip details. For example: “What time is our flight?” “Which hotel are we staying at on Day 3?” “What should I pack for Hallasan hiking?” Beyond the chatbot, TripSquad also includes: ✈️ Smart itinerary population Paste raw itinerary text, and AI helps convert it into structured trip activities. 📸 Group photo sharing Everyone can upload and view trip memories in one shared gallery. 🎬 Vlog creation Turn shared photos and videos into simple trip vlogs. 👥 Group collaboration Invite friends, share trip links, and keep everyone synced. One interesting learning I had towards the end of the hackathon was around the chatbot implementation. Initially, I thought I needed a full RAG approach. But for this MVP, I realised the trip context is usually small enough to store in the database and pass directly to the LLM when needed. With modern LLMs supporting larger context windows, this is simpler, faster to build, and good enough for the first version. The takeaway for me was: Not every AI feature needs RAG from day one. Start simple, understand the data size and user flow first, then introduce RAG only when retrieval actually becomes necessary. This project was built using v0 and ChatGPT as part of the hackathon workflow — from shaping the idea, designing the user flow, and quickly turning the concept into a working prototype. Big thanks to the organizers for creating a space where builders can experiment, learn, and ship quickly. Looking forward to building more practical AI products from here. #AIEngineer #Hackathon #RAG #v0 #ChatGPT #Vercel #TravelTech #SingaporeTech

* Just wrapped my first ever AI hackathon: the SSEN (Swedish Student Entrepreneurship Network) Hackathon in Gothenburg. My team built "Backhaul Copilot" for the Einride challenge. The problem: Einride's electric trucks complete a Gothenburg–Stockholm delivery and then drive 471 km back empty, wasting energy, capacity, and generating unnecessary emissions. Our solution automatically discovers, scores, and ranks freight companies along the E4/E20 corridor as potential backhaul partners, so those return trips become revenue miles instead of dead weight. Full stack, with FastAPI backend, React frontend, a three-pillar scoring engine pulling from OpenStreetMap and the Swedish business registry, interactive map, revenue estimates, and one-click outreach emails. 3 cups of coffee, ~4000 lines of code, and 5 effective hours of coding. We didn't leave anything on the table. First hackathon for me, and I get why people get hooked. There's something about a room where everyone's heads-down on a tough problem that's hard to find elsewhere. --- Now the part I can't stop thinking about. Almost every team in our challenge group built essentially the same thing. Same core features, same UI aesthetic: clean, polished, and almost interchangeable. I went and asked the Einride judge about it afterwards: Does he, as someone who actually wants to use the best solution, prefer diversity or convergence? His answer surprised me a little. He prefers convergence because it means every team correctly identified and tackled the core problem. For this specific challenge, I think he's right. The problem was well-defined, just technically hard to solve. Convergence is a reasonable signal that teams understood what mattered. But one of the other challenges at the event asked teams to design an AI-native business ecosystem - open-ended, no concrete deliverable required. Convergence there would've been a failure, not a feature. Problem type matters. Still, food for thought: when almost everyone in the room is using the same AI tools, are we accelerating good problem-solving, or just producing the same solutions faster and more polished than before? At the same time, none of the teams could have delivered so much functionality without AI. Hackathons have always been about rapid iteration and unexpected ideas. The output quality has never been higher. But I'm not sure the thinking has ever been more uniform. Learning for next time: basic functionality will always converge. The only way to stand out is to build the one feature nobody else thought to ship, and actually present it well. First hackathon done. Definitely not the last. Shoutout to my team Zinnie Pham Nilsson, Luca M., Mahdi Afarideh, Dat Nguyen; and to Lovable for sponsoring.

Over the next year or two, you'll hear about new AI tools constantly. My honest advice is to engage with that selectively rather than compulsively. Before diving into a new tool, it's worth pausing to think about what outcomes you actually need to achieve, and whether this particular tool is genuinely well suited to helping you get there. Your preferred LLM is actually quite good at helping you think that through, which has a certain logic to it. Signing up to everything and then working backwards to find a use case tends to lead to a graveyard of unused subscriptions and a vague feeling of being permanently behind. Starting from outcomes tends to be more useful. With that said, I'd genuinely love to know what you're using Manus for at the moment, or which AI tools have actually earned their place in your workflow lately. Let me know in the comments 👇

* Most AI approval flows ask you one question. Approve or Deny? We think that's the wrong question entirely. This weekend, I joined the XDesign Club × Superchat × Lovable hackathon at CODE University of Applied Sciences The challenge: design the moment an AI agent pauses and asks a business owner for the go-ahead before taking a real action - a refund, a booking change, an upgrade. 10 seconds. On mobile. Mid-shift. We chose a hotel scenario. Meet Arjun - the hotel manager, currently checking in a guest at the front desk. His AI agent Lily is on WhatsApp with Maria, a returning guest who just confirmed she wants a room upgrade. It's €255 above Lily's auto-approve threshold. Lily can't do this alone. Arjun's phone buzzes. Here's what we asked ourselves: What does Arjun actually need to see in that moment? What does Maria feel while she's waiting? And what happens if Arjun doesn't respond at all? The answer we're building isn't Approve / Deny. It's clarity and control in one place - → Who Maria is. Her history. The risk level. → What Lily recommends. → Ways to respond - approve, cap it, whisper an instruction, modify, take over, defer, or deny gracefully. All in under 10 seconds. And on Maria's side? She's never sitting in silence. Lily is talking to her the whole time - warm, on-brand, keeping her calm. The detail I'm most proud of: After every decision, the agent gets smarter - One tap and it learns. Arjun never sees the same request twice. That's the future of human-AI collaboration and we got to design it in 3 hours. HOW COOL IS THAT. Thank you to my amazing team Sharan Thakur and Maria Sole Biondi. And a huge thank you to Superchat for a brief that genuinely made us think, and to CODE University of Applied Sciences for organising an event that felt anything but first-edition. 🔗 Prototype: https://lnkd.in/d-kEXmxn #XDesignClub #Superchat #Lovable #Hackathon #AIDesign #UX #ProductDesign #AgenticAI #CODEUniversity #BuildingInPublic

posts.text: AI Engineer Event 1/3 completed !! 🚀 Thank you to 65labs and the team for bringing this event to life. As always, thank you Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh for organising such an insightful event. Today’s sessions made one thing very clear: AI engineering is rapidly evolving from simple chatbots into production-grade agent systems. Some key takeaways: • 🌐 Real-time research agents now go beyond basic RAG with live search, crawling, monitoring, and structured reasoning workflows. • 🤖 AI coding workflows are shifting towards “software factories” — orchestrating multiple agents, parallel tasks, MCP integrations, and evaluation loops. • 💳☁️ Building AI products is no longer just about inference; monetisation, deployment, and production infrastructure matter too. • 📊🔍 Evals, tracing, and observability are becoming critical for improving reliable agent behaviour in production. Biggest takeaway for me: The future is not just “AI helping humans code” — it’s humans designing systems where multiple AI agents collaborate, evaluate, and improve workflows together. Lots of practical and production-focused learning around agents, workflows, evals, and AI systems today. Can’t wait for the next 2 days 👀 #AgenticAI #LLM #RAG #MCP #AiEngineer #softwarefactory #evals

Brought MyKo into this world during the 65labs x AI Engineer Hackathon this weekend. MyKo is a desktop presence — a small black cat who lives on your screen, watches what you're doing, and occasionally shares her snarky thoughts about it. 📸 That's her in the screenshot — sitting on the side of the desktop, reading a Kubernetes architecture PDF, and concluding there's nothing to summarize. The architecture: → Gemini Vision reads the screen every 30 seconds and returns a one-sentence description of what's happening → GPT-5.5 receives that description alongside session memory and decides whether MyKo has anything to say → Change detection compares each screenshot against the last — if nothing has changed, the API call is skipped entirely → Document awareness is page-scoped: when a document is open, Gemini reads the visible page — what the user is actively looking at — rather than ingesting the full file. MyKo's awareness is naturally bounded by the user's own attention. → Observations persist across sessions in a local memory file, giving her context that accumulates over time. You can find MyKo napping here : https://lnkd.in/gti4tkyH --- Thank you to my teammates Sardor Madaminov and Amelia Low - it was genuinely easy to work with both of you, and I'm glad we found each other at the venue. A huge thank you to the hosts Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Adlin Zainal, Nehal Agrawal, Brian C., Daren T., and sponsors for putting this together. The standard set by every team in that room was genuinely inspiring. Looking forward to more such hackathons and events. #AIEngineer #Hackathon #GenAI #Singapore #LLM #GeminiVision #GPT5 #OpenAI #ElectronJS #AIAgents #PromptEngineering #AIHackathon
