posts.text: AI Engineer Singapore is officially sold out. ten days before we start. this conference is our love letter to the singapore tech scene. for years, we have felt that singapore deserved better AI events. the appetite was always here. the people were always here. but singapore kept getting treated like a place for regional marketing, sales, and business roles, not a place where serious builders live. that never felt right to me. when i first found the scene in 2013, it was alive. meetups every week. hackathons all the time. startup open houses where you could just show up and meet people building things. i still remember meeting someone from RedMart on a friday evening, just after they had raised their first $400k. hackerspace was around. older builders were running events constantly. if you were young and curious, there was a lot to learn from. then, slowly, it faded. i still do not really know when or why. by the time AI arrived, the scene felt different. too much of the oxygen went to people who wanted to be seen talking about AI, not people who were actually making things with it. that was not the scene I fell in love with. for the last two years, my crew and i with 65labs have been trying to bring some of that back. we were teaching people to code with AI in 2024, when half the room had not heard of claude. we ran meetups and hackathons under 65Labs. the biggest cursor hackathon in the region. we ran and supported hackathons for DeepMind and OpenAI. mostly, we just kept showing up and doing the reps. AI Engineer Singapore is what all of that was building toward. and it's not just the 3 days. the leadup has turned into a full singapore summer of AI - we're hosting quality meetups, workshops, hackathons, demo nights all over the city with some of the best companies and our dearest friends. full lineup at www.aievents.sg. this is the first conference in the region built around actually getting your hands dirty. every ticket includes a full day of workshops, because there is no point talking about AI if you are not using it. the rest of the program has the same taste: practical, direct, and built for people who ship. no thought leadership theatre. no "future of AI" panels from people who have not built anything. no roadshow energy. builders talking to builders about what actually works. selling out ten days early feels good. of course it does. but mostly, it makes the hunger impossible to ignore. singapore wants this. maybe it always did. and it is a reminder to us too: this community deserves better than the events it usually gets. to everyone who trusted a first-time conference in Singapore enough to buy a ticket, thank you. genuinely. you took a bet on us before we had proven anything. we will make it count. see you on may 15. Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Adlin Zainal Kaspar Hidayat Ivan Leo Gabriel Chua Congrats team AI Engineer Sg, for pulling off an event of this scale for AI in this region! I would look up to you all AI builder champs to be in Batam in August and build some useful stuff there too. Batam Innovation Center needs all the support to bridge the two regions Absolutely brilliant seeing engineering on center stage again … well done Agrim :) So proud of y’all Sweet stuff! And totally looking forward to geek out for the weekend! Legends, bringing power to the people! Best organisers in Singapore. Absolutely cracked team so sick man! Congrats team!!

posts.text: Thank you, Gabriel! Last week, I won the “Feel the AGI” award at the Codex OpenAI Hackathon. Built in under 4 hours, so definitely a prototype. But the idea was simple and useful: Why should comparing cab fares in Singapore still be manual? For the same ride, prices across 7 taxi / ride-hailing aggregators can differ by SGD 1 to SGD 25, depending on the time of the day and driver load. But opening every app, entering pickup and drop-off, waiting for quotes, and comparing options is tedious. So most people don’t. A consumer should just get the best price. I used Codex to build a cab fare comparison agent. The interesting part was not "Can AI click mobile buttons correctly?" but deciding what should be automated and what should be reasoned through. Pure automation is fast, but brittle. One ad, search suggestion, inconsistent app flows, keyboard, or layout change can break the flow. Pure GenAI is flexible, but using a model for every tap is slow, expensive, and unnecessarily nondeterministic. So I built a hybrid loop. Automation moves quickly through known app flows. GenAI steps in only when interpretation is needed: reading the screen, dismissing overlays, choosing the right field, resolving location suggestions, or deciding the next action. The intent-classification layer kept the task bounded: select pickup, select destination, retrieve fare. No “AI wandering around the phone.” Just constrained execution, visual checkpoints, and recovery when the UI got messy. Latency also needed different kind of framing- for this task, the user doesn't necessarily want to see through every tap happen live rather the result should be completed in background- which shifts the priority to accuracy, auditability, and recoverability at first. The demo had almost no UI by design- just wanted to make the execution loop finer, not build another dashboard. Small Singapore use case. Bigger pattern for consumer automation. Thanks to OpenAI and the Codex hackathon team. This one was fun. Demo link in comments. #OpenAI #Codex #AI #Agents #Automation #GenAI #Singapore #Hackathon EMERGENCY CODEX HACKATHON ✅✅✅ Some of my favourites from today: > using Codex’s Computer Use to compare ride-hailing options (Sahil Sharma) > GPT Image 2 for public education infographics on emergency response (Manoj Bhardwaj) > extending the open source hatch pet skill for game sprites (Reynaldo Wijaya Hendry, Akilesh Jayakumar) Thank you Brian C. for co-hosting this with me, and to everyone who came by, built something, broke something, and nerded out about Tokenmaxxing & Codex. See y’all tomorrow for Codex Hack Night: Frontend & Design with Cleon W. And more at the AI Engineer Hackathon this Saturday 🥃 Agrim Singh , Sherry Jiang , Rachael De Foe , Ivan Leo , Kaspar Hidayat , Nehal Agrawal , 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan OpenAI ❤️ Singapore

Singapore's Foreign Minister just published the architecture of his personal AI assistant on GitHub. His name is Dr Vivian Balakrishnan — a trained eye surgeon who somehow ended up as one of the very few sitting ministers in the world who actively writes code. He calls the project NanoClaw, and it runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 sitting in his home network. Here is what the Pi does. It reads his WhatsApp and Gmail. It transcribes voice notes locally, so audio never leaves the network. It builds a knowledge graph from every speech, article and conversation he feeds it. Claude is the reasoning engine on top. When asked how he built it, he gave the line worth remembering. 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐥𝐲, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐯𝐢𝐛𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠. He never opened an IDE. Claude Code made every edit. His job was to connect the right pieces together until they worked. The pieces are not exotic. A Pi 5 costs around ₹10,000 in India. The local voice and embedding tools are free and open source. The Claude API is metered but cheap for one person. A sitting foreign minister, with off-the-shelf parts, shipped the kind of personal AI agent companies are still drafting strategy documents about. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐬? 😀 Excellent work, Vivek—this is the direction the world is heading. From an India perspective, the bigger challenge is deployment in rural schools where internet access is limited or absent. There’s a strong case for building offline-first AI systems tailored for such environments. That’s where the next wave of impact lies. 😊

Singapore Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan built NanoClaw — a self-hosted Claude AI second brain running on Raspberry Pi, with persistent memory and WhatsApp/Telegram integration. Open source. At the CNBC Converge Live fireside chat on April 22, 2026 — the day after publishing NanoClaw — Balakrishnan discussed Singapore's balance between the US and China, the Hormuz crisis supply chain impact, and explicitly framed AI as a strategic diplomatic tool. The timing of the NanoClaw publication alongside his public appearances was deliberate: he was demonstrating, not just describing. His quote from the GitHub gist: "The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge." What NanoClaw Actually Is NanoClaw is a personal AI agent built from open-source components and documented for replication. The core stack: Base model: Anthropic Claude via API. Balakrishnan chose Claude specifically — the gist documentation notes Claude's reasoning quality and instruction-following as the reasons. The assistant name "NanoClaw" is a direct reference to the underlying model (Claw = Claude). Hardware: Raspberry Pi. Self-hosted, not cloud-dependent. The Pi runs the orchestration layer — managing memory, routing messages, scheduling tasks, and calling the Claude API. Compute-intensive inference still goes to Anthropic's servers via API; the Pi handles everything else locally. Messaging integrations: WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord. The assistant is accessible via any of these channels — you message it as you would message a person. It processes both text and voice notes (voice is transcribed before being passed to Claude), and can handle images. The multimodal input means a diplomat can photograph a document, ask a question about it, and receive analysis instantly. Persistent memory system: The critical architectural piece. Standard LLM conversations are stateless — the model forgets everything between sessions. NanoClaw implements a structured memory layer: facts, context, policy positions, historical precedents, and prior conversations are stored and retrieved to give Claude session-to-session continuity. For a diplomat where institutional knowledge accumulates over years, this compounding memory is what makes the system genuinely useful rather than a novelty. Scheduled tasks: The assistant runs recurring tasks on a schedule — daily briefings compiled from specified sources, reminders, summaries of ongoing negotiations or policy tracks. Set once, runs continuously. Security hardening: Hardened deployments isolate NanoClaw within Docker or Apple Containers, preventing the agent from accessing the host operating system. This is the security boundary that makes running an AI assistant with access to sensitive context tolerable from an infosec perspective. https://lnkd.in/gYp5eefV # Singapore FM Dr Vivian Balakrishnan's AI Assistant NanoClaw

A recent article about Singapore’s Foreign Minister, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, and his custom “second brain” for diplomacy has been circulating among my peers. It’s a fascinating look at how a leader can delegate cognitive load to a trusted digital system. Progressive and interesting work. You can read the article here. https://lnkd.in/gUpS3WB4 It also highlights a critical distinction that many are missing. A “second brain” is a passive extension of your own mind. The AI agents that businesses are rushing to deploy are intended to be active extensions of your will. And that changes the security conversation entirely. This is the gap I see in nearly every AI strategy session I sit in on across the region. We are building active agents on a passive trust model. The result is a new, subtle form of risk that boils down to three core problems: 1. The "Trusted Servant" Illusion We think of the agent as a trusted servant, like the "second brain." But the moment it acts sending an email, updating a record it stops being a passive library and becomes an active participant in your business processes. Its actions have consequences, but its authority is often dangerously implicit. 2. The "Delegation Black Hole" The "second brain" works because the delegation is simple: it holds your data for you. But how do you delegate authority for an agent to act across three different systems on your behalf? Most setups can't do this securely, creating a black hole where accountability and audibility simply disappear. 3. The Lack of an Actionable Mandate The agent is given a task, but it has no clear, persistent "mandate" that travels with it. It might be verified at the start, but that authority erodes as it moves through a complex workflow. This leaves the agent operating on assumptions a risk no leader should be comfortable with. We can't build a future of automation on a foundation of implied trust. It has to be explicit. That’s why my team and I have consolidated our observations into a simple, non-technical blueprint for how leaders can securely adopt AI. It's not a product pitch. It's a strategic framework for moving from the passive "second brain" model to an active, secure, and governable "second pair of hands." Happy to discuss it with any other leader navigating this challenge. The link is in the comments. Thanks for sharing, Dan. The collision of words... Fascinating: Singapore’s Foreign Minister just published his personal AI architecture. He’s running his AI second brain on a Raspberry Pi, while most CEOs are still asking ChatGPT to summarize PDFs 😳 Vivian Balakrishnan shared the full setup behind NanoClaw, his self-hosted AI assistant for diplomatic work. It sits on a Raspberry Pi 5 and connects his notes, speeches, briefings, voice memos, research, and messaging workflows into a persistent memory system. Most people still use AI like a vending machine: Ask question. Get answer. Forget everything. Repeat tomorrow. Balakrishnan is using it like infrastructure 🧠 A system that remembers. Synthesizes. Recalls context. Compounds over time. The stack is surprisingly practical: → Raspberry Pi 5 for local hosting → NanoClaw for agent orchestration → Obsidian for human-readable knowledge → SQLite knowledge graph for structured memory → Local embeddings through Ollama → whisper for on-device voice transcription → Docker containers for isolation → Claude Code to assemble the whole thing The key thing here is that he did not build this by becoming a full-time software engineer. He described it as “tool assembly.” And that may be the new executive skill. ↳ Not writing every line of code. ↳ Not outsourcing every workflow to vendors. ↳ But knowing what to combine, what to keep private, and how to make your knowledge system improve every week. This is where AI at work is heading. → From chatbots to second brains. → From prompts to workflows. → From software subscriptions to personal infrastructure. My takeaway here is this: The next productivity gap will not be between people who use AI and people who don’t. It will be between people using rented intelligence and people building owned memory. Because when everyone has access to the same models, the real moat is the context & the data only you control. P.S. check out how I Turned Claude Cowork Into My Personal COO that does work while I sleep 🧠: https://lnkd.in/eS6JCk2G More like a second faulty brain. This setup is fundamentally broken, but for a completely different reason. The fatal flaw is that it relies entirely on Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern. Yes the local hardware might function, however the memory architecture itself is a recipe for silent data corruption. The system works by allowing an AI to constantly rewrite and summarise mutable markdown files in the background. This removes the human completely from the verification loop. If the model hallucinates a single detail during a routine background update, that hallucination permanently overwrites the previous knowledge. Because there is no human curation and no strict audit trail for these changes, small hallucinations will inevitably compound over time. The system will eventually poison its own memory pool, making it far too unreliable for serious executive or diplomatic work. Thx Feels like the real shift isn’t just from tools to infrastructure but from answers to memory that actually shapes decisions. A system can store everything but if it doesn’t change how decisions get made day to day, it’s still just a better archive. Curious where you see that boundary when memory starts becoming leverage, not just storage. The "rented intelligence vs owned memory" framing is good, but it stops short of the real question. A self-hosted Claude assistant with no operator controls, handling diplomatic work, running 24/7 -- that's not just a productivity tool. That's a governance gap waiting to close at the worst possible moment. Tool assembly is the new executive skill. Runtime accountability is the one nobody's talking about yet. the owned memory vs rented intelligence line nails it, doesn’t it? once everyone has the same models, the edge is the context only you as a user can control. that could be the real moat in the end... same shift is hitting finance teams. those that own their data will run circles around teams just renting capability through saas. The more universal the models become, the more personal the advantage becomes. When everyone has access to the same intelligence, the edge shifts to the context only you control. When I sat down 3 months ago to build NanoClaw as a personal tool to help me run my company's sales pipeline, I never imagined a foreign minister would use it to help him do international diplomacy at the highest level 🤯 Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan shared a detailed technical writeup over the weekend of the personal AI system he built on NanoClaw and runs on a Raspberry Pi. It connects to his WhatsApp and Gmail, transcribes voice notes locally, ingests speeches and articles, and builds up a knowledge graph over time. He says he doesn't dare switch it off. He composed four open-source pieces: NanoClaw, mnemon, OneCLI, and Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern. He composed existing tools but created something that is uniquely his. What struck me most wasn't what he built. It's what he did next. He didn't keep it internal. He didn't treat it as Singapore's edge. He wrote it up and put it on GitHub. His words: "The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge. I think that edge is now." When I said as much publicly, he responded with something that's stuck with me: he called what he did "tool assembly." Not coding. Not building from scratch. Assembling the right tools into a system that works for his domain. That's what NanoClaw itself is at its core. Just composition of open-source tools. The thesis is that the assembly is the valuable act, not the individual pieces. There are tens of thousands of professionals building setups like this right now. Doctors, lawyers, researchers, investors. The impulse will be to sit on it. Resist that impulse. By publishing, you become a beacon. Other people working on the same things find you. They share what they're building, suggest improvements, point at things you didn't know existed. You learn faster. You stay in the center of where things are happening. Publishing isn't giving away your edge. It's doubling down on it. This is what real leadership looks like. Taking the initiative to wire up these tools directly into everyday apps and open-sourcing the process shows that the best way to understand the technology is to build it yourself. Amazing hands-on work. It's official - NanoClaw is legit! Wow! We can learn a lot from Singapore The beacon point lands hard - publishing pulls others in, and you learn faster. Worth adding: that same logic applies to governance. As more leaders build assemblies they "don't dare switch off," we'll need to learn from each other on where the final call must remain human. Collectively, that's how we make this a safer space to build in. No one builds from zero. We've always relied on layers: libraries, frameworks, supply chains. Car makers don't make their own tyres. What's changed is the speed of assembly, and how much one person can build and run before needing a team to scale it. Even if you're Singapore's Foreign Minister. Not an ordinary foreign minister, apparently.in case you are not aware of - he was a leading eye doctor (ophthalmologist) before joining politics. I spent 7 hours building a visual novel where the NPC is genuinely thinking. There are no dialogue options. You just type what you say to her. You arrive in a dying town. One person knows the safe route through the mountain pass. She doesn't share it with strangers. She notices when you contradict yourself. She warms up slowly, if at all — and some people never get the map. What surprised me most was watching people play it. There's a moment when Mara references something you said three turns ago, or goes quiet in a way that feels loaded, and players just... stop. They start choosing their words more carefully. They start wondering what she actually thinks of them. That's the thing I was chasing. Not a smarter chatbot in a game, but an interaction where the other person feels real enough that you care how it goes, and which changes the direction of the narrative. The stack: GPT-4o by OpenAI for Mara's dialogue, ElevenLabs for her voice (generated live each turn, mood-aware), Lyria powered by Google Gemini for the game's music that shifts as the conversation does, and Ren'Py as the game engine — with the backend deployed on Vercel. The Last Cartographer is on itch.io if you want to try it out. Fair warning — she's not easy to win over. https://lnkd.in/gWPvWSPZ Password in the comments! Demo video: https://lnkd.in/geV2qCdW Built solo at AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore this weekend — thanks to Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh from 65labs, and the organising team for putting it together, and to the sponsors whose credits made it possible: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Cursor, and Vercel, along with the other numerous companies who made it happen! posts.text: Fires have been making headlines in Singapore with worrying regularity. For most of us, an alarm means grabbing our things and walking out. For an elderly resident, a person with a disability, or someone recovering from illness — that walk may not be possible. And in any one block, it's rarely just one neighbour who could use a hand. SCDF will always be the professionals. But in those first critical minutes before help arrives, the people best placed to act are often already inside the building — fellow residents, a few floors away. That's why I'm spending tomorrow at the AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore building Fire Kaki — a community safety network where a vulnerable resident's SOS reaches on-duty volunteer neighbours within a 2 km radius, instantly. ("Kaki" because help should come from the people next door, not strangers a city away.) The prototype display the core flow: SOS, dispatch, four-role permissions, audit trail. See it in action: https://lnkd.in/gAZemG3h I'm looking for like-minded builders to take it further with me tomorrow. Winning a prize would be a bonus; what I really want is to leave the venue with something that could one day help a real auntie or uncle in our own neighbourhood — or a few of them at once, when minutes matter most. Huge thanks to 65labs, Sherry Jiang, Agrim Singh, and Adlin Zainal for hosting and for the relentless work behind the scenes. #AIEngineer #Hackathon #Singapore #TechForGood #BuildInPublic #AIforGood

Fires killed 5 people in Singapore last year — up from 3 the year before. Many were seniors, alone at home. For most of us, an alarm means grabbing our things and walking out. For an elderly resident, a person with a disability, or someone recovering from illness — that walk may not be possible. And in any one block, it's rarely just one neighbour who could use a hand. SCDF will always be the professionals. But in those first critical minutes before help arrives, the people best placed to act are often already inside the building — fellow residents, a few floors away. Jalan Besar GRC saw this and acted. Their Fire Safety Kakis programme trains neighbours to help evacuate vulnerable residents before SCDF arrives — and the model works. What's missing is a platform: most rosters today live on paper or in chat groups, without verification, GPS targeting, or an audit trail. That's why I spent the weekend at the AI Engineer Hackathon Singapore building 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐊𝐚𝐤𝐢 with Volodymyr I. — a community safety network that turns informal volunteer rosters into a real-time, location-aware response system. A vulnerable resident's SOS reaches on-duty volunteer neighbours within 2 km, instantly. Web, WhatsApp, iOS, and Android — so no one is excluded by device or comfort with apps. ("Kaki" because help should come from the people next door, not strangers a city away.) The prototype shows the core flow: SOS, dispatch, four-role permissions, audit trail. → https://firekaki.sg Win or no win, this doesn't end at the hackathon. As Vice Secretary of the Selegie–Waterloo Residents' Network, I'll be taking Fire Kaki to work with Jalan Besar GRC (Josephine Teo Wan Rizal Bin Wan Zakariah Shawn Loh, CFA Denise Phua) — bringing it from prototype to the ground, where the aunties and uncles actually live. We're looking for like-minded builders to take this further. Got 15 minutes yesterday with the founder whose AI framework Singapore's Foreign Minister uses as his second brain. Gavriel Cohen is the creator of NanoClaw. For a minister to go on stage and say, I use NanoClaw because it's secure by default and feel free to hack my system, that's bold. Then Gavriel's talk followed and he articulated well how their NanoClaw agent factory speeds up code review with human-in-the-loop approvals. I had to pick his real brain. Three things I walked away with. 1️⃣ When the headlines for an agent are blaring security alerts, CISOs are not going to stick their neck out to adopt them. You need to give assurance that the agent has zero risk of doing something badly. NanoClaw's stance is "don't give agents the ability" in the first place. While I agree in principle, this is going to take real work to constrain the tools they have access to. 2️⃣ Design for distribution. Even in the agentic AI era, this hasn't changed. Pick a vertical you already have a wedge into and get your first customers from there. Not the vertical you find most interesting. The one where you already have the relationships, the credibility, or the lived experience to walk in warm. 3️⃣ Local models for memory compaction may not be reliable enough yet. Compressing context with a small model risks losing the load-bearing detail and distorting what the agent acts on later. For an enterprise that needs everything to run on-premise, that compromise may still be necessary. A quick session, but speaking with a founder who's gotten global traction gave me real insight into how AI leaders are thinking about these problems. Gavriel was very gracious to make his agentic calendar public. I hope in Singapore we get to connect with more founders and speakers this way to learn from the best. I find Gavriel Cohen's insights on NanoClaw's secure-by-default approach crucial for AI adoption. Prioritizing robust security and strategic vertical distribution is paramount for transformative technology to achieve scalable impact, driving industry innovation. Michael Hart any insights/lessons learnt on credential handling, especially on progressive scoping and MCP related? Strong insights from a proven operator. Security-first agent design and vertical wedge distribution are exactly how enterprise AI adoption happens. Systems thinking always beats feature excitement.

Singapore is apparently obsessed with AI. Here you have the foreign minister self-hosting Claude on a Raspberry Pi and building a diplomatic knowledge graph using Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Wiki pattern. Running locally on NanoClaw by Gavriel Cohen 🤯 Is this the future we are walking into? Prags Mugunthan this feels less like “using AI” and more like building your own operating system for thinking and decision making 🤯 Most people are still opening a tool, asking a question, and closing it, and nothing carries over (been there). This is something that builds context, connects dots, and gets sharper over time. The Raspberry Pi setup also says a lot. It’s not about DIY for the sake of it, it’s about pulling AI out of generic tools and turning it into something that’s actually yours. Prags Mugunthan This feels like a real inflection point, not the models themselves, but who is using them and how. When AI becomes a “second brain” that compounds over time (not just a tool you query), it shifts from productivity layer → decision-making infrastructure. The Raspberry Pi detail is what stands out. It removes the “only big tech can do this” narrative entirely. The barrier isn’t access anymore—it’s mindset. I see this less as obsession and more as a global transition.In Korea, many universities and workforce training programs are also rapidly adding AI-related education.The bigger challenge is not access to AI tools anymore—it’s helping people connect them to real operational problems.Technology moves fast, but practical adoption still depends on people, processes, and clear use cases. If this is where a foreign minister lands in 2026, the question for any organisation is not whether to do this. It is why they have not started. Prags, the change is visible. A foreign minister self-hosting on a Raspberry Pi and choosing open-source tells us where AI adoption is heading. The interesting part is that a senior government official prioritised local control and ownership over convenience. Prags Mugunthan This goes beyond productivity. It’s about augmenting judgment with a structured memory system. This feels like early infrastructure shift.

A country's foreign minister builds an AI second brain to handle diplomatic complexity Here's what almost nobody noticed: this system is a personal knowledge graph. It just isn't called that. The story: Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore's Minister for Foreign Affairs, published the full architecture of his personal AI assistant this weekend. It runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 under his physical control. It ingests his WhatsApp, Gmail, and voice notes. It extracts discrete facts into a graph database - Mnemon, a graph-native memory backend - and synthesises them into structured wiki pages. Semantic recall runs on every query. The system doesn't just retrieve; it builds context over time. The stack: \* NanoClaw (agent orchestration by Gavriel Cohen and Lazer Cohen - amazing story and top of my list) \* Mnemon (knowledge graph memory) \* OneCLI (credential proxy), and the LLM Wiki pattern. All open-source. Sovereignty by design. The killer line from Balakrishnan: he doesn't dare switch it off. When a serving diplomat's personal AI becomes load-bearing infrastructure, the architectural choices start to matter. The bit I want to zoom in on: this is a de facto personal knowledge graph. In 2023, Ivo Velitchkov and I published Personal Knowledge Graphs, the first book on the topic. We argued that a new generation of tools - not necessarily built on traditional KG approaches - was converging toward something deeply familiar: individuals building connected knowledge structures, edge by edge, link by link, over years. Three years later, that convergence is accelerating. Mnemon. Mem0's graph memory layer. cognee. And an ever-rising tide of graph memory backends. Some are lightweight, embeddable, personal-scale graph databases designed for agent state. PKGs in everything but name. And the people adopting them don't even need to know the term knowledge graph to benefit. Others aim at enterprises. But this goes beyond the standard definition of knowledge graphs, in which "enterprise" was everything but spelled out. For close to a decade I've been tracking all things graph. This emerging Graph + AI / Agent Memory frontier is the fastest moving edge I've seen. Nobody has fully mapped it yet. That's what we're building at State of the Graph: https://lnkd.in/dVpyC4EC The Personal Knowledge Graph Book called this: https://lnkd.in/dMJ7tjEE Have you used a personal knowledge graph without calling it that? And now that a foreign minister trusts one, does that change how seriously you take the pattern? → Graph vendor trying to stand out in this fast-moving space? I help tech companies build visibility before the category gets crowded. → Technologist evaluating graph memory backends or building your own agent stack, and you want a map of the landscape before you commit? Let's compare notes. → Investor or analyst looking to chart this market and spot the next breakout? DM me. Great! (though I'm not a fan of the image) Impressive capability—but this is exactly where structure matters. What’s being shown is a powerful Performer (AI) executing full activity chains. The risk isn’t failure—it’s authority drift and expertise erosion. Transparency and inspectability help, but they’re not enough. Visibility ≠ governance. What’s missing is: -Explicit human authority over lifecycle stages -Controlled decision context and definitions -Persistent knowledge capture from each run Without that, humans shift from decision-makers to observers—and capability atrophies. The opportunity is bigger than “AI that works fast.” It’s AI whose every action becomes governed, traceable, and reusable knowledge—so capability compounds instead of disappearing. That’s the difference between automation… and sustainable intelligence. Ellie Rofe thats interesting case to check it out Great analysis my friend! State of the Graph look very cool.

I wasn't expecting a Minister for Foreign Affairs to share his AI insights at a Tech event.🤯

When you think of a Minister for Foreign Affairs, you probably don't picture someone running a personalized AI agent off an old Raspberry Pi. But Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan's recent keynote is full of surprises. Before his long career in politics, he was an eye surgeon, and he remains an avid tinkerer who assembles watches and reprograms appliances in his spare time.

His perspective on AI is incredibly grounded and practical. Here is a quick takeaway of his core points on adopting AI tools:
- ​Tool Assembly over Coding: You don't necessarily need to write complex code to build something useful; you can assemble existing open-source tools (like Nano Claw, Ollama, and Obsidian) to turbocharge your own productivity
- Learn by Doing: You cannot effectively govern or utilize a technology you have only been briefed on. You have to get your hands dirty and experiment with the tools yourself

Watch the full video here: https://lnkd.in/gTKpmzRC

​#AIEngineerSG #TechInSG #ArtificialIntelligence #Productivity #AITools #AgenticAI #SingaporeTech #VivianBalakrishnan
